Thus:

> **After the Scripture-appeal He returns to the works; they seek to take Him. The remainder of the scene is context. It does not cancel the appeal, and it does not become a second works-file.**

# 59.33 Positive Warrant: This Passage Opens Christ's Verdict on the Graphē

The positive warrant can now be stated with full force, without a stack of postponements.

Christ is the Truth already identified. He confirms received Scripture already. The Graphē has standing as the written Word already. In this public controversy He is charged with blasphemy for claiming oneness with the Father. He answers by appealing to what is written in their law, citing Psalm 82:6, treating that wording as a written case concerning those to whom the word of God came, asserting in the unit that the scripture cannot be broken, and applying the case to Himself as the Father’s sanctified and sent Son. That act is a judgment upon the Graphē: the written Scripture is the court of the dispute, not an illustration, not a preference, not a later institutional ornament.

The warrant is a conjunction.

**Who argues:** the historical Person already shown to be the Truth, whose works bear witness, who confirms Scripture.

**Where He argues:** a named public Temple controversy, under stones, answering a named charge.

**What He argues from:** a received writing, γεγραμμένον in their law, identified as Psalm 82:6, named as ἡ γραφή.

**How He argues:** question, citation, case, statement of standing, application — a forensic structure.

**What that act is:** the opening of His verdict on the Graphē.

Remove any member, and the opening does not remain intact. Remove who He is, and the appeal is one more Second Temple citation. Remove the charge, and the citation is a lemma. Remove the writing, and the claim is without this court. Remove the structure, and the passage is a heap. The conjunction is the warrant.

The warrant does not wait for Chapter 63 in order to be a warrant. Chapter 63 will answer why the scripture cannot be broken. This chapter answers that He treats the scripture as the court whose wording governs the answer to blasphemy. That answer is already full. It is not the later answer. Full at this level is not premature at the next level.

Thus:

> **The investigator is warranted, with full force, in receiving John 10:34–36 as the opening of Christ’s verdict on the Graphē: He argues from the written Word’s standing as decisive in the dispute, not from mere opinion.**

# 59.34 What the Passage Explicitly Establishes at This Stage

The record is explicit on the following, and this chapter claims them as explicit.

- Jesus answered those who had named blasphemy and taken up stones (John 10:31–34).
- He asked whether it is not written in their law (John 10:34).
- He cited the wording “I said, Ye are gods” (John 10:34).
- That wording is the wording of Psalm 82:6 (identification of citation; the psalm’s sentences are themselves explicit as psalm).
- He spoke of those to whom the word of God came as those called gods (John 10:35).
- He said the scripture cannot be broken (John 10:35).
- He applied the case to the one the Father sanctified and sent, restating their “Thou blasphemest” and His “I am the Son of God” (John 10:36).
- The scene is the Dedication controversy in the Temple, after “I and my Father are one,” after works named as witness (John 10:22–30).
- After the Scripture-answer He returned to the works, and they sought to take Him (John 10:37–39).

Those are not inferences from a theory of inspiration. They are the passage and its stated context.

Thus:

> **What is explicit is the answer, the writing, the citation, the case, the statement about the scripture, the application, and the Dedication controversy that contains them.**

---

# 59.35 What the Passage Does Not Yet Establish

The same honesty requires a list of what this chapter does not claim to have finished, not as doubt about the opening, but as the shape of the movement.

- It has not exposited Psalm 82 in the psalm’s own context, nor shown in full why this wording is the wording He uses (Chapter 60).
- It has not followed His reasoning from the written wording as the dedicated object, nor stated in full the weight He assigns to that wording (Chapter 61).
- It has not defined “broken,” nor answered why the scripture cannot be broken from what Scripture is (Chapters 62–63).
- It has not examined John 17:17, “thy word is truth,” as Graphē-doctrine (Chapter 64).
- It has not concluded that the Graphē is the primary written authority by which truth is known, tested, reasoned through, taught, discerned, and lived (Chapter 65).
- It has not written Movement IX’s mishandling-files, nor Movement X’s labour-files, nor the Six First Principles.

The list is sequence. Sequence is not a second conclusion that the opening is weak.

Thus:

> **The opening does not consume the later files. The later files do not postpone the opening. Each question remains its own question.**

# 59.36 Competing Claim: Proof-Texting Without Context

The first live reduction is proof-texting without context.

The reduction says: John 10:35b is a convenient sentence; quote it; the doctrine of Scripture is finished.

The reduction fails for reasons already in the passage.

The clause stands inside an answer to a charge. Without the charge, the clause is not what it is in John. Without the citation, the clause is not attached to a written wording. Without verse 34, the clause is not an appeal to their law. Without verse 36, the clause is not applied. A convenient sentence is not the complete passage.

The reduction also fails as architecture. The locked guidance for John 10 requires context, quotation, identification of the psalm, reasoning, explanation of “cannot be broken,” and the why. A proof-text is the refusal of that guidance. This chapter is steps 1–2 of the arc, not the refusal of the arc.

Proof-texting is not the same act as quotation. This chapter quotes. It quotes the complete unit. It locates the unit in the controversy. Quotation in context is the remedy for proof-texting, not an instance of it.

Thus:

> **Proof-texting without context fails. The clause is an answer in a dispute. A detached slogan is not John 10:34–36.**

---

# 59.37 Competing Claim: The Passage as Only About “Gods”

The second live reduction is topical capture by the word “gods.”

The reduction says: the interesting thing in John 10:34–36 is a debate about deification, human judges, or later metaphysical systems; the Graphē is incidental.

The reduction fails because the first move of the answer is not a theory of gods. The first move is “Is it not written.” The material is a written wording. The characterization is those to whom the word of God came. The parenthetical is about the scripture. The application is about blasphemy and the Son of God. “Gods” is the cited vocabulary. It is not the passage’s only object, and it is not this movement’s title.

Chapter 60 will have to treat “Ye are gods” with full seriousness in Psalm 82’s context, because Christ treats that wording with full seriousness. Seriousness about the wording is not capture of the passage by a later topic. Capture would skip the writing in order to reach a preferred controversy about the word “gods.” This chapter refuses the skip.

The reduction’s motive is understandable. The word shocks. Shock is not a method. Method is: He asked whether it is written; He cited; He applied. The Graphē is not incidental to that method. It is the method’s court.

Thus:

> **The passage is not only about “gods.” It is an argument from a written wording in a blasphemy-dispute. The wording matters as writing. Topical capture fails.**

---

# 59.38 Competing Claim: This Chapter as Already Chapters 62–65

The third live reduction is architectural theft.

The reduction says: once John 10:34–36 has been quoted, “cannot be broken” is finished, John 17:17 is finished, and the Graphē is already the primary written authority in the Movement VIII sense.

The reduction fails because quotation is not the dedicated why, and one controversy’s appeal is not the finished gate.

Chapters 62–63 must examine what “broken” means and why the conclusion holds from what Scripture is, not merely from the fact that Jesus quoted a clause. That is the locked assignment. This chapter has quoted the clause as part of the unit. It has not performed that assignment.

Chapter 64 must examine “Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth.” That sentence is not in John 10:34–36. Neighbourhood in the Gospel of John is not identity of assignment.

Chapter 65 must draw the conclusion earned by the whole preceding argument of Movement VIII. An opening cannot be a conclusion of an arc that has not yet been walked.

The reduction’s attractiveness is haste. Haste would close the book at the first appearance of a useful sentence. The manuscript’s rule is the opposite: earn the conclusion through the argument. This chapter earns the opening. It refuses to steal the close.

Thus:

> **This chapter is not already Chapters 62–65. Quotation of the unit is the opening. The dedicated why, John 17:17, and the Graphē-gate remain later questions.**

---

# 59.39 Competing Claim: This Chapter as a Retry of Chapter 45 or 48

The fourth live reduction is duplication disguised as thoroughness.

The reduction says: Chapter 45 already treated John 10; Chapter 48 already noted the appeal; therefore this file is a digest.

The reduction fails because those files reserved this object.

Chapter 45 treated the works-argument and expressly reserved the Scripture-argument of John 10:34–36 for Movement VIII. Using the works as context is obedience to that reservation, not a retry of the works.

Chapter 48 treated confirmation as general practice and expressly reserved John 10 as a dedicated argument, because the why of “cannot be broken” must rest on what Scripture is, and because the argument of John 10 is an argument, not a slogan. Performing the opening of that argument is obedience to that reservation, not a second confirmation-file.

A digest would repeat those chapters’ conclusions under a new heading. This chapter uses those conclusions as premises and examines the complete passage as the new object. Shared vocabulary with a new function is not duplication. “John 10” in Chapter 45 names works. “John 10” in Chapter 48 names an instance of practice. “John 10:34–36” in this chapter names the unit and its controversy as the opening of the Graphē-verdict. The name is shared. The function is not.

Thus:

> **This chapter is not Chapter 45 retried and not Chapter 48 retried. Those files reserved this object. Performing the reserved object is not duplication.**

# 59.40 Reason Through the Evidence

The inference can now be inspected.

**Step 1.** The Dedication scene is a public controversy: demand for plain speech, works as witness, claim of oneness with the Father (John 10:22–30). Explicit.

**Step 2.** The opponents take up stones and name blasphemy: being a man, He makes Himself God (John 10:31–33). Explicit.

**Step 3.** He answers by asking whether it is written in their law and by citing “I said, Ye are gods” (John 10:34). Explicit. The cited wording is Psalm 82:6. Identification of citation.

**Step 4.** He treats the citation as a written case about those to whom the word of God came, and states that the scripture cannot be broken (John 10:35). Explicit as His speech. Dedicated sense of “broken” reserved.

**Step 5.** He applies the case to the Father’s sanctified and sent One, against the charge of blasphemy for saying He is the Son of God (John 10:36). Explicit as application; dedicated logic reserved.

**Step 6.** The form of Steps 3–5 is an appeal to a received writing as the court of the dispute, not an appeal to mere opinion. Inference from form and placement, warranted by the explicit question “Is it not written.”

**Step 7.** Given already that He is the Truth who confirms Scripture, and given already that the Graphē has standing as the written Word, this act is the opening of His verdict on the Graphē. Inference from the act plus premises already in force.

**Step 8.** The live reductions fail: proof-text without context; topical capture by “gods”; theft of Chapters 62–65; duplication of Chapters 45 and 48.

**Step 9.** Therefore the investigator is warranted in receiving the complete passage, in this controversy, as Movement VIII’s first word: Christ argues from the written Word’s standing as decisive in the dispute.

The inference is not: Jesus quoted a verse; therefore every later Graphē-doctrine is finished. That inference would be a non sequitur and a theft. The inference is: Jesus answered a blasphemy-charge by opening their written Scripture as court; therefore this is the opening of His verdict on the Graphē, at the level that act warrants.

Thus:

> **The reasoning is inspectable: controversy, charge, written appeal, cited psalm, case, statement of standing, application; therefore opening of the verdict; later files remaining later.**

The distinction must be kept clean.

The conclusion may now be stated without apology and without theft.

# 59.43 The Scope of This Stage

The scope of this stage is the complete passage and its argumentative context as the opening of the verdict.

Inside the scope: the Dedication controversy; the demand; the works as context; the oneness-claim as prompting the charge; the accusation of blasphemy; the complete quotation; “written in your law”; the naming of Psalm 82:6; the structure of the three verses; the appeal as decisive in the dispute; the appeal as not mere opinion; the failure of the live reductions; the positive warrant for treating this as Movement VIII’s first word.

Outside the scope, by assignment, not by evasion: Psalm 82’s own context and the reason this wording is used; the dedicated logic and weight of the written wording; “cannot be broken” as finished doctrine and why; John 17:17; the Graphē-gate; Movements IX–X; First Principles; *spoudazō*.

The scope is the chapter’s honour. A chapter that pretends to finish the arc at the first step has not honoured the passage. A chapter that refuses to finish its own step until the arc is complete has not honoured the passage either. This chapter finishes its step.

Thus:

> **The scope is John 10:34–36 in context as opening. What lies outside the scope remains outside because it is a different question.**

---

# 59.44 Apply the Standard

The master formula required definitions, distinctions, premises, biblical record, evidence, competing claims, reasoning, explicit versus inferred, a warranted conclusion, and the next question. Those operations have been performed.

The four governing questions have not been conflated. The ontological question — what stands in this scene as the court of the dispute — has been answered as the received written Scripture, the Graphē named as ἡ γραφή. The epistemological question — how that court is known in the scene — has been answered by His question “Is it not written,” the citation of wording, and the opponents’ own possession of the law. The evidential question — what warrants treating this as the opening of His verdict — has been answered by the conjunction of who He is, what the Graphē has been shown to be, and what He does with the writing under a blasphemy-charge. The hermeneutical question — how the cited psalm is to be understood in its own context, and how the later reader is to handle an authoritative text — remains later. Chapter 60 will handle the psalm. Movement IX will handle mishandling. The present file has not pretended to be those files.

The Easton test has been applied in its proper analogue. A later writer may say that John 10:35 is a proof-text, or only a curiosity about gods, or already the whole doctrine of unbreakable Scripture, or already the Graphē-gate, or a retry of confirmation. The manuscript has not accepted those sentences as premises. It has asked what the passage itself presents, what the controversy is, and what the record actually warrants.

Source material has been reconstructed rather than cited as authority. The argument that the received writings function in this scene as already Scripture, and that γραφή here names Holy Writ as standing writing, has been used as inspectable reasoning tested against the text. Unverifiable historical colour has not been converted into premises.

Circularity has been refused. The argument is not: the Bible is authoritative because the Bible says it is authoritative; therefore John 10 finishes the book. The argument is: this Person, already identified, in this controversy, appeals to this writing as court; therefore the verdict on the Graphē opens here.

Prematurity has been refused. The chapter has not consumed Psalm 82 exposition, the dedicated reasoning, “cannot be broken,” John 17:17, or the Graphē-gate.

Duplication has been refused. Works remain Chapter 45. Confirmation remains Chapter 48. Synthesis remains Chapter 58. The present function is the dedicated examination of the complete passage and its context. Shared terms with a new function are not duplication.

Thus:

> **The standard required for a chapter of this book has been applied. John 10:34–36 has been examined as a complete argument in context. The next necessary question is the cited wording in its own Psalm.**

---

# 59.45 From the Passage to the Cited Wording of Psalm 82:6

A complete passage, now examined in its controversy as an appeal to what is written, still leaves a further question.

The opening is in force. He has asked whether it is written. He has cited “I said, Ye are gods.” The wording has been named as Psalm 82:6. Those sentences are the cleared ground. They are not yet the dedicated examination of the citation and the psalm’s context.

If the wording were not located, the next question would be which writing He meant. The wording is located. If this chapter were already that later examination, the next file would be repetition. This chapter is not that later examination. The next question is therefore the construction the locked assignment names: the actual citation and its Psalm 82 context, and why Christ uses the written wording.

That is the proper open of the next chapter. John 10:34–36 was never meant to be a slogan about gods, and it was never meant to finish Movement VIII at the first step. It was meant to be the complete argument in context, sufficient to justify taking the next question, which is the question a cited writing itself forces once it has been named.

---

# What Has Been Established

This chapter has established:

1. **John 10:34–36, in this argument, is a complete unit of answer, not a proof-text fragment, not a slogan, and not the whole of Movement VIII.**
2. **Argumentative context is the Dedication controversy: public Temple scene, demand for plain speech, works as witness, “I and my Father are one,” stones, and the named charge of blasphemy.**
3. **The works-argument of John 10 remains Chapter 45’s object, used here as context, not retried.**
4. **The accusation is blasphemy: being a man, He makes Himself God. The Scripture-argument is the answer to that charge.**
5. **The hinge of the scene is the turn from stones as the opponents’ court to what is written as Christ’s court.**
6. **The complete quotation has been given in full argumentative force: verses 34, 35, and 36 together.**
7. **He appeals to what is written: “Is it not written in your law…?” The appeal is to a received writing, as written, as the court of the dispute.**
8. **“Your law” names the received written Scripture they already acknowledge, including this wording; it is not unwritten custom, and it is not the Graphē-gate.**
9. **The cited wording is Psalm 82:6. The psalm is named. Its own context remains Chapter 60.**
10. **Verse 35 treats the citation as a written case: those to whom the word of God came were called gods.**
11. **“The scripture cannot be broken” belongs to the unit as His assertion of the writing’s standing and is reserved as dedicated doctrine for Chapters 62–63.**
12. **Verse 36 applies the written case to the sanctified and sent Son against the charge of blasphemy. Dedicated reasoning remains Chapter 61.**
13. **The three verses have a forensic structure: writing asked, wording cited, case characterized, standing asserted, charge applied.**
14. **The appeal is to Scripture as decisive in this dispute: their writing, as writing, used as a case, governing the application.**
15. **The appeal is not mere opinion.**
16. **Chapter 48’s confirmation is used, not retried; this is the dedicated controversy that file reserved.**
17. **Chapter 58’s synthesis is used, not retried; standing of the written Word is premise, not a second join.**
18. **Neighbouring “it is written” cases illuminate the practice and neither isolate nor absorb this scene.**
19. **After the Scripture-appeal He returns to works; they seek to take Him. Remainder is context.**
20. **Positive warrant: this passage opens Christ’s verdict on the Graphē. He argues from the written Word’s standing, not from mere opinion.**
21. **Proof-texting without context fails.**
22. **Treating the passage as only about “gods” fails.**
23. **Treating this chapter as already Chapters 62–65 fails.**
24. **Treating this chapter as a retry of Chapter 45 or 48 fails.**
25. **What is explicit has been distinguished from what is inferred, and later doctrines have not been inferred here.**
26. **This chapter opens Movement VIII because its first assigned word has been stated.**
27. **This chapter opens Chapter 60 by naming the next necessary question without answering it.**
28. **What is reserved is Chapter 60 in full; Chapter 61 in full; Chapters 62–63 in full; Chapter 64 in full; Chapter 65 in full; Movements IX–X; First Principles; and σπουδάζω (*spoudazō*).**

---

# Chapter Summary

> **The chapter’s central conclusion:** John 10:34–36, read as a complete argument in the Dedication controversy, is Christ’s appeal to what is written as decisive in a dispute over blasphemy. He has claimed, “I and my Father are one.” They take up stones and charge that, being a man, He makes Himself God. He answers from their law, citing “I said, Ye are gods” — the wording of Psalm 82:6 — treating the wording as a written case, asserting in the unit that the scripture cannot be broken, and applying the case to Himself as the Father’s sanctified and sent Son. The appeal is to the Graphē as court, not to mere opinion, not to a fragment, and not to a slogan. Competing reductions fail: proof-texting without context; the passage as only about “gods”; this chapter as already Chapters 62–65; this chapter as a retry of Chapter 45 or 48. The investigator is warranted, with full force, in receiving this passage as the opening of Christ’s verdict on the Graphē. Psalm 82’s own context remains later because it is a later question. Movement VIII is open. The first verdict of Movement VIII is in force.

The essential architecture is:

> **Standing of the written Word already stated → complete passage defined → context as accusation, works, and blasphemy-charge → appeal to what is written defined → opening of the verdict named → lexical control → Dedication scene from the record → works used, not retried → oneness-claim as prompt → charge named → complete quotation → “your law” → Psalm 82:6 named and reserved → structure exhibited without consuming later files → positive warrant → failure of reductions → first verdict warranted → sequence to Psalm 82.**

The governing distinctions are:

- **Complete passage** is not **proof-text fragment**.
- **Argumentative context** is not **isolated slogan**.
- **Appeal to Scripture** is not **the Chapter 65 gate**.
- **Naming Psalm 82:6** is not **Chapter 60**.
- **Exhibiting structure** is not **Chapter 61**.
- **Quoting “cannot be broken”** is not **Chapters 62–63**.
- **This file** is not **Chapter 45 retried**, not **Chapter 48 retried**, and not **Chapter 58 retried**.
- **Opening of the verdict** is not **completion of Movement VIII**.
- **Limits** are **the shape of the doctrine**, not **delayed doubt**.
- **Sequence** is **not hesitation about this level**.

The decisive principle is:

> **Examine the complete passage John 10:34–36 and its argumentative context, claiming what that controversy warrants and not more: Christ argues from the written Word’s standing as decisive in a blasphemy-dispute, citing Psalm 82:6, not from mere opinion, before expositions of the psalm, before the dedicated reasoning-file, before the finished why of unbreakability, before John 17:17, and before the Graphē-gate. Draw the conclusion the premises support. Do not draw the conclusions that still require later premises. Then ask what the cited wording is in Psalm 82.**

---

# Transition to Chapter 60

Movement VIII is open. Its first word has been stated.

The central witness has been located in history, identified as the Truth, authenticated in claims and works, examined at the hinge of death and raising, attested by positioned seers, shown to confirm the Scriptures He received, shown to send apostles, and shown to authenticate the New Testament witness as continuous with earlier Scripture. The body of writings so treated has been identified, recognized, grounded, exhibited as one testimony, distinguished as to operations, warranted as inspired record, shown not to fail as record, and synthesized as the written Word of the God who cannot lie. That written Word has now been heard in a particular controversy: John 10:34–36, the Dedication scene, the blasphemy-charge, the appeal to what is written in their law.

The writings that present that appeal do not leave unused the further question of the wording He cites. The passage has named the citation by quoting it. The citation has been located as Psalm 82:6. Location is not the psalm’s own context, and it is not the dedicated account of why He uses this written wording. The next necessary question is therefore not a new curiosity. It is the actual citation and the Psalm:

> **What is the written wording “I said, Ye are gods” in Psalm 82:6, now that John 10:34–36 has been shown to be an argument from that wording in a blasphemy-dispute, and now that the next file’s first word is to be the psalm’s own context rather than a slogan about gods?**

That is the subject of:

# Chapter 60 — “I Said, Ye Are Gods” — Psalm 82:6

> **Examine the actual citation and its Psalm 82 context. Reason through why Christ uses the written wording.**

The investigation now moves from:

> **the complete passage John 10:34–36 in its argumentative context**
>
> to:
>
> **the cited wording in its own Psalm.**

# End of Chapter 59

chapters.title: “I Said, Ye Are Gods” — Psalm 82:6
chapters.body:
> **Movement VIII — Christ's Verdict on the Graphē**

> **Central objective:** Examine the actual citation and its Psalm 82 context, and reason through why Christ uses the written wording — not as a fragment divorced from the psalm’s argument, not as a slogan about “gods,” not as the dedicated file of His reasoning from that wording to the Son-claim, not as the finished doctrine that the scripture cannot be broken, not as John 17:17, and not as the Graphē-gate. This continues Movement VIII. It is not Chapter 59 retried, not Chapter 61 written in advance, not Chapters 62–65 written in advance, and not a blank check for later speculation about the word “gods.”

---

## Chapter Assignment

Chapter 59 established Movement VIII’s first word. John 10:34–36, read as a complete argument in the Dedication controversy of John 10:22–39, is Christ’s appeal to what is written as decisive in a dispute over blasphemy. He has claimed, “I and my Father are one.” The opponents take up stones and charge that, being a man, He makes Himself God. He answers by asking whether it is not written in their law, citing “I said, Ye are gods,” treating that wording as a written case concerning those to whom the word of God came, stating in the unit that the scripture cannot be broken, and applying the case to Himself as the one the Father sanctified and sent. The cited wording was named as Psalm 82:6. Naming is not exposition of the psalm. The appeal is to the Graphē as the court of the dispute, not to mere opinion, not to a proof-text fragment, and not to a slogan about “gods.” That opening is already in force. Movement VIII is open.

Chapter 59 ended by naming the next necessary question, not a new curiosity:

> **What is the written wording “I said, Ye are gods” in Psalm 82:6, now that John 10:34–36 has been shown to be an argument from that wording in a blasphemy-dispute, and now that the next file’s first word is to be the psalm’s own context rather than a slogan about gods?**

That is this chapter’s assignment.

The locked Table of Contents states the work in two sentences:

> **Examine the actual citation and its Psalm 82 context. Reason through why Christ uses the written wording.**

The locked John 10:34–36 guidance assigns ten steps to the arc as a whole. This chapter is steps 3–4 of that arc, now performed rather than merely begun: identify Psalm 82:6 as the cited writing in the writing’s own context; give the relevant Psalm text. It also performs the assignment’s second sentence: reason through why He uses the written wording rather than a paraphrase that would weaken the case. It does not follow Christ’s dedicated reasoning from that wording to the present charge as Chapter 61’s object. It does not explain “the scripture cannot be broken.” It does not ask why it cannot be broken as the finished why. It does not connect that why to John 17:17 as finished Graphē-doctrine. Those later steps remain later because they are later questions. Naming them is not performing them.

The chapter does not re-prove that God cannot lie. It cites Chapters 11–12 as established. It does not re-prove γραφή as writing that, in biblical usage, designates Holy Writ. It cites Chapters 20–22 as established. It does not re-try Christ’s historical place, identity as the Truth, or the claims-and-works conjunction. It cites Chapters 43–45 as established. It does not re-try confirmation of received Scripture as Movement VI’s dedicated file. It cites Chapter 48 as established. It does not re-try corpus, recognition, inspiration, infallibility, or the Movement VII synthesis. It cites Chapters 51–58 as established. It does not re-try the Dedication controversy, the complete passage as a unit, or the naming of the citation. It cites Chapter 59 as established. It does not treat Christ’s reasoning from what is written as finished. It does not treat “cannot be broken” as a concluded “why.” It does not treat John 17:17 as finished Graphē-doctrine. It does not claim that the Graphē is primary written authority in the Movement VIII sense. It performs the examination without which those later files would reason from an unidentified fragment rather than from a psalm.

A complete passage, now examined as an appeal to what is written, still leaves a further question. What is the writing He cites, in that writing’s own argument, and why does the case require the wording as written rather than a summary that would evade the words? Naming neighbourhood is not examining the psalm. The present file is that examination, at the level the premises warrant, and not beyond it.

The remaining questions of Movement VIII follow. Sequence continues the investigation. It does not convert the present line into hesitation.

---

## Central Objective

> **To examine, from the biblical record and from premises already in force, the actual citation of Psalm 82:6 in its own psalm-context, so that Movement VIII’s second word is one inspectable conclusion: the wording Christ cites is the psalm’s own address, directed in the psalm’s frame to those who judge under God — those to whom the word of God came — and He uses that written wording because the case depends upon what stands written, not upon a paraphrase that would weaken or relocate the argument; to keep that examination distinct from the dedicated reasoning-file, from the finished doctrine that the scripture cannot be broken, from John 17:17, and from the Graphē-gate; and to refuse both under-claim and over-claim.**

The governing movement is:

> **Movement VIII’s first word already stated → question of the actual citation and Psalm 82 context → the citation defined as the written wording in its own psalm → context defined as the psalm’s argument, not a detached lemma → why written wording defined → lexical control of אֱלֹהִים and neighbouring terms → the psalm given in full → the psalm’s argument followed verse by verse → verse 6 located inside that argument → the addressees identified from the psalm’s frame and from Christ’s own characterization → judicial function in the wider biblical record used as correspondence, not as a modern controversy’s center → why a paraphrase would weaken the case → the wording as already standing Holy Writ for His hearers → positive warrant that the citation is Scripture-governed argument → competing reductions refused → inspectable inference → warranted conclusion → sequence to Christ’s dedicated reasoning from what is written.**

The chapter’s conclusion is affirmative:

> **Psalm 82, read as a complete argument and not as a fragment, is a judicial psalm in which God stands in the congregation and judges those called gods, charging them with unjust judgment, commanding defense of the poor, and declaring that they shall die like men. Verse 6 is the address already spoken: “I have said, Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High.” That address is directed, in the psalm’s own frame, to those who judge under God and who have received His word — the same characterization Christ names when He says “unto whom the word of God came.” He cites the written wording, not a paraphrase, because the blasphemy-charge concerns the vocabulary of God, and the writing already stands with that vocabulary as Holy Writ in force for His hearers. The investigator is warranted, with full force, in treating this citation as Scripture-governed argument: the psalm’s wording is the material of the court already opened in Chapter 59. It is not yet Chapter 61. It is not yet Chapters 62–63. It is not yet John 17:17. It is not yet the Graphē-gate. It is not a blank check for later “gods” speculation. Movement VIII continues. That is this chapter’s conclusion, stated here with full force.**

The remaining questions follow by sequence. The citation’s context is already in force.

---

# 60.1 The Question Created by the Preceding Chapter

Movement VIII has opened. John 10:34–36 has been examined as a complete argument in the Dedication controversy: an appeal to what is written as decisive in a dispute over blasphemy; a citation of wording; a characterization of those to whom the word of God came; a statement in the unit that the scripture cannot be broken; an application to the Father’s sanctified and sent Son. The cited wording has been named as Psalm 82:6. It has not yet been examined as that psalm’s own sentence in that psalm’s own argument, and it has not yet been shown why the written wording, rather than a paraphrase, is the material the case requires.

Chapter 59 established the opening. That conclusion is a premise here. A named citation still leaves a further question: if He cites “I said, Ye are gods,” what is that sentence where it already stands, to whom is it spoken, and why does the appeal require the words as written? Naming locates the writing. The present file examines the writing.

A people can receive the Dedication scene as a controversy, receive verses 34–36 as an answer, receive “your law” as their own writing, receive the naming of Psalm 82:6, and still leave unasked what Psalm 82 itself argues. The writings themselves force the further analysis. God stands in a congregation. He judges among gods. He charges unjust judgment. He commands defense of the poor. He says, “Ye are gods.” He says they shall die like men. Those sentences, already in the psalm, have a joint consequence concerning the citation Christ uses. If they have none, “the actual citation” is a title. If they have every consequence a later slogan wishes, the investigation has stopped reasoning.

The question is therefore not:

> **What is the argument of John 10:34–36 in its argumentative context?**

That question has been answered.

The question is:

> **What is the written wording “I said, Ye are gods” in Psalm 82, to whom is that address directed in the psalm’s own frame, and why does Christ use the written wording rather than a paraphrase?**

If Movement VIII proceeded from the naming of the psalm to the dedicated a fortiori without the psalm, it would treat a lemma as a court. If it treated this file as already Chapter 61, it would consume the later logic before the writing’s own argument has been heard. If it treated this file as already Chapters 62–65, it would consume the later why and the later gate before the citation has been examined. If it treated this file as a retry of Chapter 59, it would convert a psalm-examination into a second Dedication-file. The present file is the dedicated examination of the actual citation and its Psalm 82 context.

That is a different operation from piety. It is the operation this chapter must perform.

---

# 60.2 What This Chapter Does Not Repeat

Chapters 1–3 established truth as conformity to reality, distinct from belief, popularity, and institutional consensus. Chapters 4–7 established knowledge, evidence, reason, and rational warrant as inspectable operations. Those conclusions remain premises. This chapter does not re-write the opening epistemology. It uses truth as already defined, now as the standard against which the psalm’s sentences and Christ’s use of their wording are examined as writing, not as a pious shock.

Chapters 10–12 established that God is the ground of truth, that He is truthful, faithful, and immutable, and that falsehood is incompatible with Him. Those conclusions remain premises. This chapter does not re-write the impossibility of divine falsehood. It uses that impossibility as already in force for any later claim that the writing to which Christ appeals is God’s writing.

Chapters 20–22 established γραφή (*graphē*, G1124) as writing that, in biblical usage, designates Holy Writ / Scripture. Those conclusions remain premises. This chapter does not re-try the lexical file. It uses the term as John 10:35 uses it of the writing now under examination.

Chapters 43–45 established Jesus Christ as a corroborated historical figure, identified in the authentic testimony as the Truth and the revealer of the Father, and authenticated in claims and works, including John 10’s works-argument. Chapter 48 established His confirmation of the Scriptures He received as binding written word. Those conclusions remain premises. This chapter does not re-try existence, identity, works as witness, or confirmation as a general practice.

Chapters 51–58 established corpus, recognition, prophetic-apostolic ground, unity of testimony, distinction of operations, inspiration’s guarantees, infallibility of the record, and the synthesis of truth, authority, and the written Word. Those conclusions remain premises. This chapter does not re-try Movement VII. It uses the Graphē’s standing as written Word as already-cleared ground.

Chapter 59 established the complete passage, the Dedication controversy, the blasphemy-charge, the appeal to what is written, the naming of Psalm 82:6, the characterization “unto whom the word of God came,” the presence of “cannot be broken” in the unit, and the application to the sanctified and sent Son. Those conclusions remain premises. This chapter does not re-try the Dedication scene, the three-verse unit, or the naming of the citation. It uses that opening in order to examine the cited psalm.

This chapter does not re-describe winter and Solomon’s porch as if the scene were still unlocated. It does not recatalogue Matthew 4 and Luke 24 as if confirmation were still in doubt. It does not treat 2 Timothy 3:15–17 as a second inspiration-file. It does not invent unverifiable details of Asaph’s biography, festival reconstruction, or a later scholarly quarrel as the chapter’s center. The new function is this:

> **To examine the actual citation of Psalm 82:6 in the psalm’s own argument, and to reason through why Christ uses that written wording; to refuse both emptiness and overclaim; and to leave the dedicated reasoning, “cannot be broken,” John 17:17, and the Graphē-gate in their assigned files.**

---

# 60.3 Define the Question: The Actual Citation and Psalm 82 Context

**The actual citation and its Psalm 82 context**, in this chapter, is the written wording Christ quotes — “I said, Ye are gods” — examined as Psalm 82:6 inside the argument of Psalm 82 as a whole, together with the reason He uses that wording as written rather than a paraphrase, not as an isolated shock-phrase, not as a later metaphysical system, and not as the whole of Movement VIII.

The phrase is easily abused. In ordinary speech “Ye are gods” may mean a slogan of deification, a curiosity about Hebrew vocabulary, a weapon in later debates about identity, or a license to treat every later Graphē-doctrine as already settled because a psalm exists. None of those senses is this chapter’s object.

Four elements belong to the definition.

First, **the actual citation**. The wording He cites is not a theme, not a mood, and not a later summary. It is the sentence already standing in the psalm: “I have said, Ye are gods.” Citation is quotation of what is written. A paraphrase that reports the psalm’s “gist” is not the citation. A later expansion that adds what the psalm does not say is not the citation.

Second, **in its Psalm 82 context**. Verse 6 is not a detached proverb. It stands after God has taken His place as judge among those called gods, after the charge of unjust judgment, after the command to defend the poor, and before the sentence that they shall die like men. Context is the psalm’s argument. A fragment is not the psalm.

Third, **why He uses the written wording**. The assignment is not merely to display the psalm. It is to reason through why the case in John 10 requires this wording as written. The reason will be that the charge concerns the vocabulary of God, that the writing already uses that vocabulary of those to whom the word of God came, and that a paraphrase which avoided or inflated the words would weaken the court He has opened.

Fourth, **not those other claims**. The definition excludes, as not this object: the dedicated logic from the wording to the Son-claim as Chapter 61’s finished file; the finished sense of “broken”; the dedicated why; John 17:17 as finished Graphē-doctrine; the Graphē-gate; a retry of Chapter 59’s Dedication-file; a blank check for later speculation that every use of “gods” means what a later system wishes. Those exclusions are part of the definition. They are not a later apology.

Thus:

> **The question of this chapter is not whether John 10:34–36 is an argument from writing, whether the scripture cannot be broken, or how the a fortiori to the Son is drawn in full. Those questions have been examined or remain later. The question is what Psalm 82:6 is in Psalm 82, to whom the address is directed, and why the written wording is the material Christ uses.**

---

# 60.4 Distinguish Eight Objects That Must Not Be Collapsed

The investigation fails at the first step if it treats different objects as one.

## 60.4.1 This chapter and Chapter 61’s full logic of Christ’s argument from the writing

Psalm 82 supplies the wording. Chapter 61 will show the logic by which He moves from that wording to the present charge, and the weight He assigns to the written text. This chapter must show why the wording as written is the material. Showing why the wording is used is not drawing the dedicated a fortiori. To treat this file as already Chapter 61 would steal the later logic. To refuse to ask why He uses the written wording would leave the assignment’s second sentence unperformed.

## 60.4.2 Exposition of Psalm 82 and the finished doctrine that the scripture cannot be broken

The psalm is Scripture. John 10:35 states that the scripture cannot be broken. Chapters 62–63 will examine that statement and its why. This chapter must treat the psalm as already standing writing. Treating it as standing writing is not the finished unbreakability-file. To consume Chapters 62–63 here would steal the later why. To omit the psalm’s standing as writing would make the citation a curiosity.

## 60.4.3 Psalm context and a blank check for later “gods” speculation

The psalm uses אֱלֹהִים of those it addresses. Later systems may wish to treat that vocabulary as a license for deification, for identity-teaching detached from judgment, or for a modern controversy as the center of the file. Context is the psalm’s judicial argument. A blank check is the refusal of that argument. This chapter is the second operation, not the first.

## 60.4.4 This chapter and Chapter 59’s Dedication-file

Chapter 59 located the citation in the blasphemy-dispute. This chapter locates the citation in the psalm. Neighbourhood is not identity. The Dedication scene remains premise. The psalm is the new object. Collapse of the two would hide the psalm inside a second scene-description.

## 60.4.5 The psalm’s judicial frame and a later scholarly quarrel as the chapter’s center

Verse 1 has been read, in later discussion, as a heavenly assembly or as a human court. The chapter will follow the psalm’s own verbs of judging, the mortality of verse 7, and Christ’s own characterization — those to whom the word of God came — rather than inventing a modern controversy as the center. Noting that later readers differ is not making their quarrel the object. The object is the text.

## 60.4.6 Naming of verse 6 and the whole psalm’s argument

Chapter 59 named verse 6. This chapter must give the relevant psalm, not the line alone. A named line without the indictment, the command, and the mortality-sentence is still a fragment. The assignment is the citation in context.

## 60.4.7 This chapter and the Chapter 65 gate

This chapter establishes that the cited wording stands as written Holy Writ already in force for His hearers, and that He argues from that wording. Chapter 65 will conclude that the Graphē is the primary written authority by which truth is known, tested, reasoned through, taught, discerned, and lived. Neighbourhood is not arrival.

## 60.4.8 Image or sonship correspondence and the psalm’s judicial address

Verse 6 also says, “all of you are children of the most High.” Genesis 1:26–27 records that God made man in His image. Correspondence of sonship-language is real and may be named. Correspondence is not a conversion of Psalm 82 into a later identity-lesson that ignores unjust judgment and death like men. The psalm remains a judicial address.

Thus:

> **The actual citation in Psalm 82’s context is this chapter’s object. It is not Chapter 61, not finished unbreakability, not a blank check for “gods” speculation, not Chapter 59 retried, not a modern quarrel as center, not a detached lemma, not the Graphē-gate, and not an identity-lesson that evacuates the judicial frame.**

---

# 60.5 Premises That May Be Used, and Premises That May Not

The chapter may use, as already in force:

- Truth as conformity to reality, distinct from belief, popularity, and institutional consensus (Chapters 1–3).
- Knowledge, evidence, reason, and rational warrant as inspectable operations (Chapters 4–7).
- God as the ground of truth, truthful, faithful, immutable, and incapable of falsehood (Chapters 10–12).
- γραφή (*graphē*, G1124) as writing that, in biblical usage, designates Holy Writ / Scripture (Chapters 20–22).
- Revelation given; inspiration of Scripture as writing; “all Scripture”; the sequence from communication to written testimony (Chapters 29–32).
- Authentication of the record as testimony (Chapters 33–42).
- Christ as historical, the Truth, authenticated in claims and works, crucified and raised, attested by positioned seers (Chapters 43–47).
- Christ’s confirmation of received Scripture as binding written word, including Law, Prophets, and Psalms (Chapter 48).
- The scriptural corpus, canon as recognition, prophetic and apostolic authority, unity of written testimony, distinction of operations, inspiration’s guarantees, infallibility of the record, and the synthesis of truth, authority, and the written Word (Chapters 51–58).
- John 10:34–36 as a complete argument in the Dedication controversy: appeal to what is written, citation named as Psalm 82:6, characterization of those to whom the word of God came, statement that the scripture cannot be broken belonging to the unit, application to the sanctified and sent Son (Chapter 59).

The chapter may not use, as if already finished:

- Christ’s reasoning from what is written as Movement VIII’s dedicated file (Chapter 61).
- The finished sense of “cannot be broken” and the dedicated “why” of that statement (Chapters 62–63).
- John 17:17 as finished Graphē-doctrine (Chapter 64).
- The Graphē as primary written authority in the Movement VIII sense (Chapter 65).
- Mishandling, tergiversation, ἄπειρος (*apeiros*, G552), σπουδάζω (*spoudazō*, G4704), and readiness for the Six First Principles.

The chapter may name those later questions as later. Naming is not consuming.

Thus:

> **Premises already earned may be used. Later verdicts may not be borrowed as if the citation-file had already become the dedicated reasoning, the finished why of unbreakability, or the Graphē-gate.**

---

# 60.6 The Sequence of Levels: One Clean Scope Section

What this chapter does not settle is a matter of sequence, not of doubt about what it does settle.

The investigation proceeds by levels. Each level answers its question with full force. The next level remains next because it is a different question.

**Already in force.** God cannot lie. Revelation has been given and authenticated. Scripture as writing is God-breathed. The record does not fail as truthful divine writing of what it actually communicates. The Graphē has authority as the written Word at the level earned through Movement VII. Christ is the historical Truth who confirms the Scriptures He received. John 10:34–36 is His appeal to what is written as decisive in the Dedication blasphemy-dispute. The cited wording has been named as Psalm 82:6.

**This level.** Given those premises, Psalm 82 is a judicial psalm whose verse 6 addresses as gods those who judge under God and to whom the word of God came. Christ uses that written wording because the case depends upon the words as written, already standing as Holy Writ for His hearers, not upon a paraphrase that would weaken the court. The warrant is full at this level. It is not postponed until Chapter 61 in order to keep the present conclusion weak.

**Next levels, named once.** Christ’s reasoning from what is written belongs to Chapter 61. “The scripture cannot be broken,” and why, belong to Chapters 62–63. John 17:17 belongs to Chapter 64. The Graphē as primary written authority belongs to Chapter 65. Skill, diligence, mishandling, and the First Principles remain later still.

**Limits that belong to this level itself, not to later hesitation.** The psalm’s context is not a fragment. Exposition of the psalm is not the dedicated a fortiori. Treating the wording as standing writing is not the finished why of unbreakability. The judicial frame is not a blank check for later “gods” speculation. Using Chapter 59 is not rewriting it. Those limits are part of what the citation-file is. They are not a stack of clauses designed to drain the positive conclusion.

The chapter will therefore state the positive warrant with full force, locate the limits as belonging to the doctrine rather than as apologies, and name later files once as later files. It will not repeat, under every paragraph, that the present conclusion is not proof of a later conclusion. Sequence is already the account of that difference.

Thus:

> **The present examination is in force at this level. Later verdicts remain later because they are different questions. Limits named here are the shape of the doctrine, not a delayed doubt about the doctrine.**

---

# 60.7 The Actual Citation Defined

**The actual citation**, in this chapter, is the written wording Christ quotes as already standing in their law, identified as Psalm 82:6, given in the words the writing uses rather than in a later summary of what the writing is “about.”

John 10:34:

> **“Is it not written in your law, I said, Ye are gods?”**

Psalm 82:6:

> **“I have said, Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High.”**

The citation is the first clause of the psalm-verse, in the form He quotes. The remainder of the verse belongs to the psalm’s context and will be examined with it. The citation is not less than the quoted words. It is not more than the quoted words plus the psalm that contains them.

Three false substitutes must be refused.

**A theme.** “The psalm is about judgment” may be true as a summary and still not be the citation. He does not ask whether a theme is in their law. He asks whether this wording is written.

**A later doctrinal expansion.** “Ye are gods” does not, by being cited, become a completed metaphysics of deification, a completed anthropology of image, or a completed Christology of the Son. Those expansions, if they come, must come by later argument. They do not come by the mere fact of quotation.

**A reconstructed original setting offered as the citation.** A later reconstruction of a court-scene, a festival, or a heavenly council may be offered as history. It is not the wording. The wording is what is written. Unverifiable reconstruction is refused as a substitute for the text.

The Greek of John 10:34, ἐγὼ εἶπα θεοί ἐστε, corresponds to the wording of the Greek Psalter at this verse. The correspondence is named as correspondence of written wording, not as an invented account of which physical copy He held. The argument depends upon what is written, not upon a reconstructed book-object in the porch.

Thus:

> **The actual citation is the written wording “I said, Ye are gods,” as Psalm 82:6 already stands. A theme, a later expansion, and an invented setting are not the citation.**

---

# 60.8 Psalm 82 Context Defined

**Psalm 82 context**, in this chapter, is the argument of the psalm as a whole: speaker, addressees, charge, command, address of verse 6, mortality-sentence, and closing appeal — the frame in which verse 6 is an address and not a proverb torn out of a book.

A psalm-context is not a caption. It is the sequence of sentences that makes verse 6 do the work it does. Remove verses 1–5, and “Ye are gods” has no judicial charge behind it. Remove verse 7, and the address has no mortality to qualify it. Remove verse 8, and the psalm has no appeal from failed human judgment to God’s judgment of the earth. The relevant text is therefore the psalm, not the fragment.

Context so defined is not a historical novel of Asaph’s career. The superscription names “A Psalm of Asaph.” The name locates the writing among the psalms so ascribed. It does not license a biography beyond the record. The investigation follows the sentences.

Two false substitutes must be refused.

**Immediate verbal neighbourhood without the argument.** One may quote verse 6 and call verses 5 and 7 “context” while still treating verse 6 as a slogan. Neighbourhood of words is not yet argumentative context. Argumentative context is the psalm’s case: God judging those who judge.

**A later controversy offered as context.** Later readers have disputed whether the “gods” of verse 1 are heavenly beings or human judges. That dispute may be noted as a later reading. It is not the psalm’s context. The psalm’s context is the psalm’s own verbs, addressees, and outcome. Christ’s characterization in John 10:35 is then the governing identification of those addressees for the citation’s use: those to whom the word of God came.

Thus:

> **Psalm 82 context is the psalm’s judicial argument as a whole. It is not a slogan’s caption, not invented colour, and not a later quarrel substituted for the text.**

---

# 60.9 Why Written Wording Defined

**Why Christ uses the written wording**, in this chapter, is the inspectable reason the case requires the words as they stand written, rather than a paraphrase, a theme, or a later restatement that would weaken or relocate the argument.

The definition has four elements.

First, **as written**. γεγραμμένον has already been established in Chapter 59 as the category of the appeal. The present file asks what follows for this sentence: the force is the words, not a speaker’s later equivalent.

Second, **rather than a paraphrase**. A paraphrase might say, “Scripture honours judges,” or “men have a high office,” or “God once spoke to Israel.” Each of those sentences might be related to the psalm. None of them is the wording the charge requires. The charge is that He, being a man, makes Himself God. The writing already contains “Ye are gods” as an address to those who received God’s word. Remove the word “gods,” and the writing no longer supplies the vocabulary the dispute has named.

Third, **as the material of a court already opened**. Chapter 59 opened the court. This chapter shows that the exhibit in that court is the wording. An exhibit that has been replaced by a summary is not the exhibit.

Fourth, **not the dedicated a fortiori**. Why this wording is used is not yet how the inference from this wording to “I am the Son of God” is drawn in full. The first is this file. The second is Chapter 61. The two are neighbours. They are not the same assignment.

Thus:

> **Why He uses the written wording is why the case requires the words as written rather than a paraphrase that would weaken the court. It is not yet Chapter 61’s dedicated logic.**

---

# 60.10 Lexical Control: אֱלֹהִים, εἶπα, θεοί

The psalm’s and the citation’s God-terms must be controlled, not inflated.

**אֱלֹהִים** (*elohim*, H430) is a plural form whose biblical usage includes the true God, false gods, and, in specified judicial contexts, those who sit in judgment. Lexical range is not contextual meaning. The word does not, by itself, prove deification, polytheism, or a later metaphysical system. Context must decide which use is in force in Psalm 82. The psalm itself uses the word of God who stands to judge (verse 1a) and of those among whom He judges (verse 1b; verse 6). The same form therefore appears in more than one role inside one psalm. That fact is not a license to collapse the Most High into the addressees, or the addressees into the Most High.

**אָמַרְתִּי** is the first-person perfect of אָמַר (*amar*, H559): I have said. Verse 6 presents the address as already spoken. The English of John 10:34, “I said,” and of Psalm 82:6, “I have said,” names the same completed speech. The citation is a citation of a saying already in force as said.

**θεοί** is the plural of θεός (*theos*, G2316): gods. John 10:34 quotes θεοί ἐστε — “ye are gods.” The Greek corresponds to the psalm’s אֱלֹהִים as rendered in the Greek Psalter. The term in the citation is the psalm’s term in Greek dress. It is not a new vocabulary invented for the porch.

Three refusals follow.

The terms do not, by themselves, finish Chapter 61. A named address may be located. How the Son’s argument uses that address remains later.

The terms do not, by themselves, finish “cannot be broken.” A named writing may be cited. Why it cannot be broken remains later.

The terms do not license a claim that every biblical use of אֱלֹהִים means the same thing. Context controls. Here the context is a psalm in which God judges those He has called gods, who judge unjustly, and who shall die like men.

Thus:

> **אֱלֹהִים and θεοί name, in this psalm and this citation, an address whose sense is controlled by the psalm’s judicial argument and by Christ’s characterization, not by an isolated lexicon-entry.**

---

# 60.11 Lexical Control of Neighbouring Terms Named, Not Exhausted

Other terms in the psalm must be named accurately and left, where the TOC requires, to later files or to their proper force here.

**אֵל** (*El*, H410) appears in verse 1 in the phrase commonly rendered “congregation of the mighty”: עֲדַת־אֵל, the congregation of God / El. The phrase locates the assembly as God’s assembly. It does not, by itself, settle a later quarrel about whether the assembly is heavenly or earthly. The verbs that follow will.

**עֶלְיוֹן** (*Elyon*, H5945), Most High, appears in verse 6: “children of the most High.” The title distinguishes the addressees from the One whose children they are called. Children of the Most High are not the Most High. The distinction belongs to the verse and will govern later refusals of blank-check speculation.

**שָׁפַט** (*shaphat*, H8199), to judge, is the psalm’s governing verb: He judgeth (verse 1); how long will ye judge unjustly (verse 2); do justice (verse 3); arise, O God, judge the earth (verse 8). Judicial action is not ornament. It is the psalm’s work.

**מוּת** (*muth*, H4191) underlies verse 7: “ye shall die like men.” Mortality is the psalm’s own qualification of the address in verse 6. Those called gods shall die like men. The verb forbids treating verse 6 as an ontological promotion that has no death on the other side of it.

**λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ** in John 10:35: “the word of God” came to those who were called gods. Chapter 59 named the phrase as part of the unit and reserved its mapping onto the psalm. This chapter performs that mapping so far as the psalm’s “I have said” and the addressees’ judicial commission require. It does not convert the phrase into a second inspiration-file.

**λυθῆναι** remains reserved. The unit contains “cannot be broken.” This chapter records that the writing now examined is the writing of which that clause is said. It does not define “broken.” It does not answer why.

Thus:

> **Neighbouring terms are named so the psalm is not mistranslated. Judge, Most High, die like men, and the word of God locate the frame. “Broken” remains quoted as belonging to the unit and reserved as a dedicated object.**

---

# 60.12 The Psalm Given in Full

The relevant text must be given as a complete argument, not as a proof-text fragment.

> **A Psalm of Asaph.**
>
> **God standeth in the congregation of the mighty; he judgeth among the gods.**
>
> **How long will ye judge unjustly, and accept the persons of the wicked? Selah.**
>
> **Defend the poor and fatherless: do justice to the afflicted and needy.**
>
> **Deliver the poor and needy: rid them out of the hand of the wicked.**
>
> **They know not, neither will they understand; they walk on in darkness: all the foundations of the earth are out of course.**
>
> **I have said, Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High.**
>
> **But ye shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes.**
>
> **Arise, O God, judge the earth: for thou shalt inherit all nations.**
> — Psalm 82:1–8

The eight verses are one psalm. The first sentence locates God as judge among those called gods. The next sentences charge, command, and diagnose. Verse 6 is the address already spoken. Verse 7 qualifies that address with mortality. Verse 8 appeals from the failed court to God’s judgment of the earth.

The argumentative force of the whole, at this stage, can be stated without stealing later files.

God stands. He does not leave judgment unattended.

He judges among gods. The addressees are already in a judicial frame before verse 6 is spoken.

He charges unjust judgment. The “gods” are not being flattered. They are being indicted.

He commands defense of the poor. Office is measured by justice to the weak, not by a title.

He diagnoses ignorance and darkness. The foundations are out of course. The crisis is judicial and moral, not a seminar about vocabulary.

He recalls what He has said: Ye are gods; children of the Most High. The address is prior speech, now cited inside the indictment.

He declares they shall die like men. The title does not confer immunity.

He appeals to God to judge the earth. Failed human judgment is not the last judgment.

That is the psalm in full argumentative force. A later preacher may quote only “Ye are gods.” A later controversy may quote only a theory of gods. Neither quotation is the argument. The argument is the psalm as given.

Thus:

> **The relevant text is Psalm 82 as a whole: God judging those called gods, charging unjust judgment, addressing them as gods and children of the Most High, declaring their death like men, and appealing to God to judge the earth. Fragmentation is not exposition.**

---

# 60.13 Superscription and Speaker: A Psalm of Asaph

The writing is superscribed “A Psalm of Asaph.”

The superscription locates the psalm among the Asaph psalms. It does not, in this chapter, become a biography of Asaph, a reconstructed liturgy, or an unverifiable account of first performance. The investigation takes the psalm as a writing already standing in the received Psalter, which Chapter 48 has already shown Christ to receive among the Scriptures, and which Chapter 59 has already shown Him to cite as written in their law.

The speaker of verse 1 is the psalm’s narrator presenting God as standing and judging. The speaker of verses 2–4 is God addressing the addressees. Verse 5 diagnoses their condition. Verse 6 is God’s prior address recalled: “I have said.” Verse 7 continues the divine sentence. Verse 8 is the psalm’s appeal to God.

“I have said” in verse 6 is therefore not a later commentator’s gloss. It is the psalm’s own presentation of a saying of God already in force. When Christ quotes “I said, Ye are gods,” He quotes that saying as written. He does not invent a speaker. He does not transfer the saying to a private voice of His own as if the psalm had never spoken.

The Bible Introduction’s larger argument that the received writings were already treated as Scripture in Christ’s scene is used here only as already-established correspondence: a psalm is cited as law. Correspondence is not a second confirmation-trial, and not a second canon-file.

Thus:

> **The psalm stands as an Asaph psalm in the received Psalter. “I have said” is God’s prior address as the psalm presents it. Location of the writing is not a reconstructed career of Asaph.**

---

# 60.14 Verse 1: God Standing in the Congregation, Judging Among the Gods

Verse 1 opens the frame.

> **“God standeth in the congregation of the mighty; he judgeth among the gods.”**

Two acts are named.

**He stands.** God takes His place in the assembly. The congregation is not unsupervised. Judgment is not left to those who happen to sit.

**He judges among the gods.** The addressees of the psalm are already called gods before verse 6 recalls the saying. The title, whatever its force, is already in the frame as the designation of those among whom God judges.

The verse therefore forbids two opposite errors.

**Error of flattening.** Flattening says that “gods” in verse 1a and “gods” in verse 1b must mean the same referent in the same role, so that God is judging Himself, or so that there is no Most High distinct from the assembly. The verse distinguishes the One who stands and judges from those among whom He judges.

**Error of detaching verse 6.** Detaching says that “Ye are gods” is a sudden metaphysical announcement. Verse 1 has already placed “gods” in a judicial assembly. Verse 6 will recall what has been said of those who sit there.

Later readers have asked whether the assembly is heavenly or earthly. The question may be named. It is not this chapter’s center. The verse’s own contribution is already full: God judges in an assembly of those called gods. Verses 2–7 will show what those addressees do, what they fail to do, and how they die. Christ’s own characterization will then identify them, for the citation’s use, as those to whom the word of God came.

Thus:

> **Verse 1 locates God as judge in an assembly of those called gods. The frame is judicial before verse 6 is recalled. A later quarrel about the assembly’s metaphysics is not the verse’s assignment.**

---

# 60.15 Verses 2–4: The Judicial Charge

Verses 2–4 are the indictment and the command.

> **“How long will ye judge unjustly, and accept the persons of the wicked? Selah.”**
> — Psalm 82:2

> **“Defend the poor and fatherless: do justice to the afflicted and needy. Deliver the poor and needy: rid them out of the hand of the wicked.”**
> — Psalm 82:3–4

The second-person verbs are judicial verbs. “How long will ye judge unjustly” names their office as judging and their failure as injustice. “Accept the persons of the wicked” names partiality. The commands that follow — defend, do justice, deliver, rid — are the measures of that office. The poor, the fatherless, the afflicted, and the needy are the persons by whom the court is tested.

These verses establish, with full force, that the addressees function as judges. Whatever else a later system may wish to say about “gods,” the psalm’s own sentences address them as those who judge, who can judge unjustly, and who are commanded to do justice to the weak. A reading that cannot account for unjust judgment, partiality, and the defense of the fatherless has not yet read the psalm.

The charge also establishes that the title in verse 6 is not a compliment that ends the case. The saying “Ye are gods” will be recalled inside an indictment, not as an escape from it. Office under God is compatible with failure before God. The psalm is about that compatibility, and about its consequence in verse 7.

Thus:

> **Verses 2–4 address the “gods” as judges: they judge unjustly, they are commanded to defend the poor. The judicial frame is the psalm’s own, not a later imposition.**

---

# 60.16 Verse 5: Ignorance, Darkness, Foundations Out of Course

Verse 5 diagnoses the condition of those so addressed.

> **“They know not, neither will they understand; they walk on in darkness: all the foundations of the earth are out of course.”**

Not knowing and not understanding are not compliments. Walking in darkness is not a mystical ascent. The foundations of the earth out of course is the psalm’s own measure of how serious unjust judgment is. The crisis is not a private mood. It is a disorder of the foundations.

The verse matters for the citation because it forbids treating “Ye are gods” as a statement of present competence. Those called gods, in this psalm, do not know, do not understand, and walk in darkness. The address in verse 6 is therefore not the psalm’s last word about them. It is a prior saying now set beside their failure.

Christ’s later characterization — those to whom the word of God came — is compatible with this diagnosis. The word may come, and the hearers may still not know. Receiving the word as office is not the same act as walking in the light of it. The psalm records both the coming of the address and the darkness of those addressed. Chapter 61 will use that structure so far as the dedicated reasoning requires. This chapter needs only the diagnosis: verse 6 is not a certificate of present enlightenment.

Thus:

> **Verse 5 diagnoses those called gods as not knowing, not understanding, walking in darkness. The address of verse 6 is recalled inside failure, not as a slogan of present competence.**

---

# 60.17 Verse 6: The Address — “I Have Said, Ye Are Gods”

Verse 6 is the cited wording in its place.

> **“I have said, Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High.”**

Four features of the sentence must be seen.

**It is prior speech.** “I have said” presents the address as already spoken. The psalm does not now invent the title. It recalls it. Christ’s “I said” is that recall quoted as written.

**It is second-person address.** “Ye are gods” is spoken to the addressees of verses 2–4. It is not a general proverb about the universe. It is not an abstract definition of deity. It is “ye.”

**It is the vocabulary of gods.** The word is the word. The investigation does not replace it with a weaker English substitute in order to spare later embarrassment, and it does not inflate it into a later system in order to satisfy later appetite. The writing says gods. The writing must be allowed to say it.

**It is paired with sonship-language.** “Children of the most High” stands in the same verse. The addressees are called gods and called children of Elyon. The pairing will be examined in the next section. It already shows that the verse itself supplies a relation to the Most High rather than an identity with the Most High.

At this stage, the verse’s contribution to the citation is already full. This is the wording. This is its place: after indictment, before mortality. This is its form: prior divine speech to those who judge. Chapter 59 named the verse. This section locates it inside the psalm. Location inside the psalm is the difference between a lemma and a citation in context.

Thus:

> **Verse 6 is God’s prior address to the psalm’s addressees: Ye are gods; children of the Most High. The citation is this wording in this place, not a detached shock-phrase.**

---

# 60.18 “And All of You Are Children of the Most High”

The second clause of verse 6 must not be dropped, and it must not be allowed to steal the file.

> **“…and all of you are children of the most High.”**

**What the clause is.** It is a parallel address. Those called gods are also called children of Elyon. “All of you” distributes the address across the assembly, not to one isolated figure.

**What the clause does.** It relates the addressees to the Most High as children to Father, not as rivals who have become the Most High. Sonship-language in Scripture can name Israel, can name kings, can name those who belong to God. The present verse uses it of the same persons who judge unjustly and who shall die like men. The clause therefore belongs to office and relation under God, not to an escape from God.

**What the clause does not do here.** It does not finish a doctrine of adoption. It does not finish a doctrine of the image of God. It does not finish the Son’s unique relation to the Father, already examined as identity and claim in Chapters 44–45 and applied in John 10:36. It does not become a later identity-lesson that every hearer is already “gods” in a sense that would make the blasphemy-charge unintelligible.

Genesis 1:26–27 records that God made man in His image, after His likeness. That record stands. A later leaflet-argument that places Psalm 82:6 beside Genesis 1:26 as language of man’s true nature may be reconstructed as a proposed correspondence: children of the Most High and image-language both speak of relation to God. Correspondence is not identity of assignment. Genesis 1 is the making of man. Psalm 82 is the judging of those who judge. The image does not evacuate the indictment. The indictment does not deny that man was made in the image. The two writings remain two. This chapter’s object is the psalm’s address in its judicial frame.

Thus:

> **“Children of the most High” relates the addressees to God without identifying them as the Most High. Image-language may be named as correspondence. It may not convert Psalm 82 into a blank check.**

---

# 60.19 Verse 7: Mortality and Fall — They Shall Die Like Men

Verse 7 is the psalm’s own qualification of verse 6.

> **“But ye shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes.”**

The adversative is the psalm’s. “I have said, Ye are gods” is not left without a “but.” Those so addressed shall die like men. They shall fall like a prince. The title does not confer deathlessness. The office does not confer immunity.

This verse is decisive for the addressees. Whatever later quarrel may be raised about verse 1, verse 7 names their end in the language of human death and princely fall. The psalm itself therefore places the “gods” of verse 6 on the side of those who die as men die. A reading that cannot hear “die like men” as the psalm’s own check upon “Ye are gods” has not yet read the psalm.

The verse also matters for Christ’s use. He cites verse 6, not verse 7. He does not thereby cancel verse 7. He cites the address as written. The address, in the psalm, is the address of those who remain mortal. The persons to whom the word of God came were called gods, and they remain those who die. That fact belongs to the written case. It will belong to Chapter 61 so far as the dedicated reasoning compares their calling with the Father’s sanctifying and sending of the Son. This chapter needs the qualification as the psalm’s own: the wording “Ye are gods” is not, in Psalm 82, a sentence of immortal deity.

Thus:

> **Verse 7 qualifies verse 6: those called gods shall die like men. The citation of the address does not cancel the psalm’s mortality-sentence, and the mortality-sentence forbids treating the address as a grant of deathless deity.**

---

# 60.20 Verse 8: Appeal to God to Judge the Earth

Verse 8 closes the psalm.

> **“Arise, O God, judge the earth: for thou shalt inherit all nations.”**

Failed judgment in the assembly is not the last judgment. The psalm appeals to God to arise and judge the earth. The inheritance of the nations is assigned to Him. The Most High remains the judge of the whole, not merely the supervisor of a local court.

The closing matters for context because it shows what the psalm is for. It is not a hymn to the addressees. It is a cry from their failure to God’s judgment. “Ye are gods” is not the psalm’s destination. God’s judging the earth is the psalm’s destination.

Christ’s citation of verse 6 therefore takes a line from a psalm that ends by appealing past those who were called gods. He does not cite a psalm whose point is to make men into the Most High. He cites a psalm whose point is that God judges those who judge, and that God must yet judge the earth. The later application in John 10:36 to the One the Father sanctified and sent will have this psalm, not a rival psalm, as its written material. The dedicated application remains Chapter 61. The psalm’s destination is already this file’s to state.

Thus:

> **Verse 8 appeals from the failed court to God’s judgment of the earth. The psalm’s destination is God’s judging, not the addressees’ deification. That destination is part of the citation’s context.**

---

# 60.21 The Psalm’s Argument as a Whole

The verses now stand together as one argument.

God takes His place in the assembly and judges among those called gods (v. 1). He charges them with unjust judgment and partiality (v. 2). He commands justice for the poor, the fatherless, the afflicted, and the needy (vv. 3–4). He diagnoses their ignorance, darkness, and the disorder of the foundations (v. 5). He recalls His prior address: Ye are gods; children of the Most High (v. 6). He declares their death like men and their fall like princes (v. 7). He appeals to God to judge the earth and inherit the nations (v. 8).

The argument is therefore this:

> **Those who judge under God have been addressed as gods and as children of the Most High; they have judged unjustly; they remain mortal; God Himself must judge.**

That is the psalm’s case. Verse 6 is a member of the case. It is the prior address. It is not the whole case. A reading that treats verse 6 as the whole psalm has not read the psalm. A reading that treats the judicial verbs as optional colour around a metaphysical slogan has not read the psalm.
