This is exactly the kind of intellectual posture needed for the Six First Principles.

---

## 85.52 The Graphē and Faith

Nor does scholarly labour destroy faith.

The learner does not become less faithful because he examines context.

He does not become less spiritual because he studies grammar.

He does not become less obedient because he distinguishes quotation from inference.

Faith does not require intellectual disorder.

The proper relationship is:

> **truth → knowledge → understanding → faithfulness → obedience.**

The learner should believe what God has established, not what confusion has made difficult to examine.

---

## 85.53 The Graphē and Obedience

The purpose of interpretation is not merely intellectual victory.

The learner is being prepared to live.

A correct interpretation that produces no obedience has not yet fulfilled its practical purpose.

But obedience must follow what has actually been established.

The learner should not use the language of obedience to justify an interpretation the text does not support.

Thus:

> **Interpretation precedes faithful application.**

The gate protects this order.

---

## 85.54 The Graphē and the Six First Principles

The relationship can now be summarized:

The Graphē establishes the authoritative written source.

The scholarly labour teaches the learner how to engage that source.

The workman discipline establishes accountability.

The Six First Principles provide the foundational doctrinal curriculum.

The learner enters those principles with an established relationship to the source.

Therefore the Doctrine of the Graphē is neither an optional preface nor a seventh principle.

It is the gate.

---

## 85.55 The Gate Is Necessary Because Interpretation Is Fallible

A human interpreter can be wrong.

That fact does not make Scripture uncertain.

It makes interpretation a discipline.

The learner can misunderstand.

The teacher can misunderstand.

A commentary can misunderstand.

A tradition can misunderstand.

An institution can misunderstand.

A majority can misunderstand.

A minority can misunderstand.

The existence of error therefore increases the need for disciplined engagement with the source.

It does not remove the need for authority.

---

## 85.56 Authority and Fallibility Can Coexist

The distinction is:

> **infallible source**

versus

> **fallible interpreter.**

The learner does not become infallible by entering the Foundation School.

The teacher does not become infallible by teaching the Foundation School.

The textbook does not become infallible by quoting Scripture.

The curriculum does not become infallible by being carefully constructed.

The Graphē remains the standard.

This is why the gate must remain outside the count of the six principles.

---

## 85.57 The Gate Is Not a New Revelation

Another danger must be refused.

The Doctrine of the Graphē is not a claim that a new revelation has been added to Scripture.

The book has not received a seventh foundational revelation.

It has articulated a doctrine concerning the written authority already under examination.

Its task is to establish what relationship the learner should have to the Graphē.

That is fundamentally different from adding another inspired text or another principle to Hebrews 6:1–2.

---

## 85.58 The Gate Is Not a New Canon

Nor does the present work create another canon.

The Graphē is not replaced by the book.

The book does not become an additional sacred text.

The teacher's notes do not become Scripture.

The course material does not become Scripture.

The distinction remains absolute:

> **Scripture is Scripture.**

> **Teaching about Scripture is teaching about Scripture.**

The two may be closely related in content without being identical in authority.

---

## 85.59 The Gate Is Not a New Institution of Authority

The same applies institutionally.

A school can organize study.

A publisher can distribute books.

A teacher can teach.

A platform can host courses.

An institution can certify completion.

None of these functions creates authority over the Graphē.

Institutional usefulness must not be confused with scriptural authority.

The institution serves the study.

The study serves understanding.

Understanding serves faithful handling.

The Graphē remains primary.

---

## 85.60 The Graphē Creates the Proper Order of Authority

The order can therefore be expressed:

> **God → divine revelation → written Holy Writ / Graphē → faithful interpretation → teaching and study.**

Human institutions remain downstream.

Human teachers remain downstream.

Human methods remain downstream.

Human conclusions remain downstream.

This order is the practical result of the entire manuscript.

---

## 85.61 The Book Has Been Moving Toward This Point

The conclusion should not feel like an addition.

It has been built through the entire work.

Truth required grounding.

Knowledge required evidence.

Evidence required reasoning.

Ultimate authority required a sufficient ground.

God provided the ontological ground considered in the argument.

Revelation required authentication.

The written record required examination.

The Graphē required distinction from commentary.

Authority required recognition.

Interpretation required discipline.

Skill required exercise.

Maturity required trained faculties.

The workman required accountability.

Now the prepared workman reaches the gate.

The movement has been cumulative.

## 85.63 The Six Are the Next Question

The end of this book is therefore the beginning of another inquiry.

The reader has learned to ask:

> What is the authoritative written Word?

Now he must ask:

> What does that Word teach concerning the first principles of the doctrine of Christ?

The question changes.

The source relationship has been established.

The doctrinal field now opens.

This is the correct transition.

---

## 85.64 The Graphē Has Done Its Work When the Learner Can Enter

The Doctrine of the Graphē succeeds when the learner no longer treats Scripture as merely a collection of religious quotations.

He sees it as authoritative written communication.

He knows that it must be read.

Understood.

Reasoned through.

Handled.

Tested.

Applied.

He knows that his own interpretation remains corrigible.

He knows that the teacher is not the source.

He knows that scholarship is a servant.

He knows that maturity requires work.

He is therefore ready.

That is the point of the gate.

---

## 85.65 The Learner Must Carry the Discipline Forward

The conclusion of this book does not suspend its method.

The learner should carry the method into every course that follows.

When studying repentance, he should use it.

When studying faith, he should use it.

When studying baptisms, he should use it.

When studying laying on of hands, he should use it.

When studying resurrection, he should use it.

When studying eternal judgment, he should use it.

The method does not become a seventh principle.

It becomes a disciplined way of engaging the six principles under the authority of the Graphē.

---

## 85.66 “Study” Is Now a Responsibility

The command of diligence developed in Chapter 78 now becomes concrete.

The learner is not being invited to consume religious information.

He is being called to labour.

He should read.

He should compare.

He should write.

He should reason.

He should test.

He should answer.

He should receive correction.

He should repeat the work until the material becomes skillfully handled.

This is why the Foundation School cannot be reduced to passive content consumption.

The learner must become a workman.

---

## 85.67 The First Principles Require Exercise

The work of Chapter 79 also continues.

The learner must exercise the Word.

He must use what he learns.

He must distinguish.

He must reason.

He must identify errors.

He must explain conclusions.

Repeated responsible use develops capacity.

Therefore the first principles are not merely six headings to memorize.

They are a field in which the learner's faculties are to be exercised.

---

## 85.68 The First Principles Require Maturity

Chapter 80 established that maturity is demonstrated by developed capacity.

That principle continues.

The learner should not assume that knowing the titles of the six principles means understanding them.

Nor does completing a lesson automatically mean possessing mature skill.

The learner must become capable of handling the material.

That is why the foundation is connected to the call to maturity.

---

## 85.69 The First Principles Require Discernment

Chapter 81 examined the babe and the unskilful.

Chapter 82 examined right handling.

Chapter 83 examined the approved workman.

Chapter 84 examined interpretation.

All of that now becomes preparation for the next field.

The learner should enter the Six First Principles with trained discernment.

He should be able to distinguish:

> **what is written**

from:

> **what someone says is written.**

That distinction may determine whether the foundation is laid correctly.

---

## 85.70 The Gate Is Therefore Also a Guard

A gate does two things.

It provides access.

It also regulates access.

The Doctrine of the Graphē does both.

It opens the way to the Six First Principles.

It also warns the learner not to enter them carelessly.

It says:

> Do not make the teacher the source.

> Do not make the institution the source.

> Do not make tradition the source.

> Do not make experience the source.

> Do not make your interpretation the source.

> Do not make the present book the source.

Return to the Graphē.

---

## 85.71 The Gate Prevents Doctrinal Inflation

There is another danger: doctrinal inflation.

A learner can take an explanatory distinction and elevate it into a new doctrine.

He can take a method and call it revelation.

He can take an inference and call it explicit Scripture.

He can take a theological synthesis and call it a direct biblical statement.

He can take a course structure and call it the biblical structure itself.

The Doctrine of the Graphē resists this inflation.

It requires the learner to label what he is doing.

---

## 85.72 Naming the Difference Protects the Truth

Therefore the learner should be willing to say:

> “The text says...”

> “The context indicates...”

> “The necessary inference is...”

> “A reasonable interpretation is...”

> “The broader biblical pattern suggests...”

> “This is an application...”

> “This is a historical observation...”

These distinctions do not weaken doctrine.

They protect it from exaggeration.

---

## 85.73 The Six Principles Should Be Taught With the Same Honesty

When the learner enters the six courses, the same standard applies.

A teacher should not hide a disputed interpretation behind the phrase:

> “The Bible says...”

if the Bible does not say it explicitly.

A teacher should not present an application as though it were a command.

A teacher should not present a theological synthesis as though it were a quotation.

A teacher should not present a possible inference as though it were necessary.

The gate therefore establishes a culture of intellectual honesty.

---

## 85.74 The Graphē Is the Anchor

The course material may change in presentation.

The learner may encounter different teachers.

Different editions may exist.

Translations may differ in wording.

Digital tools may change.

Methods may improve.

Historical scholarship may develop.

But the learner's governing relationship remains:

> **Return to the written Word.**

The Graphē is the anchor.

That is why the title of the present work matters.

One Source of Truth is not a slogan for intellectual simplification.

It identifies the governing written source toward which the learner is repeatedly directed.

---

## 85.75 “One Source” Does Not Mean “One Verse”

The phrase must also be understood carefully.

One source does not mean one verse.

It does not mean one isolated sentence.

It does not mean that every doctrine must be proved by a single quotation.

The Graphē is a body of written testimony.

The workman must handle its passages in context and relation.

One authoritative source can contain many books, voices, genres, contexts, arguments, and witnesses.

Unity of authority does not erase diversity of communication.

---

## 85.76 “One Source” Does Not Mean “One Interpreter”

Nor does one source require one human interpretation.

Human interpreters remain fallible.

The learner should therefore expect discussion, examination, correction, and sometimes disagreement.

The presence of disagreement does not create a second Scripture.

It creates a question of interpretation.

The proper response is to return to the source, examine the reasoning, and assess the evidence.

---

## 85.77 “One Source” Does Not Mean “No Scholarship”

The opposite misunderstanding must also be rejected.

If the Graphē is the primary written authority, it does not follow that scholarship is unnecessary.

The whole of Movement X has established the opposite.

Scholarship is necessary precisely because the source deserves serious labour.

The more authoritative the source is understood to be, the more responsibly it should be handled.

The answer to misuse of Scripture is not less scholarship.

It is better scholarship under the authority of Scripture.

---

## 85.78 The Learner Is Now at the Threshold

The workman has reached the threshold.

Behind him stands the labour of this book.

Before him stand the Six First Principles.

The correct response is neither pride nor fear.

It is readiness.

He should be able to say:

> **I know the source to which I am accountable.**

> **I know that my interpretation is not infallible.**

> **I know that I must labour.**

> **I know that I must distinguish what is written from what I infer.**

> **I know that I must be corrected.**

> **I know that I am now responsible to study the foundation faithfully.**

That is the posture of entry.

---

## 85.79 The Six First Principles Are Entered Under Authority

The learner therefore does not enter the six principles saying:

> “What does my tradition teach?”

He asks:

> **“What does the Graphē establish?”**

He does not begin with:

> “What does my teacher believe?”

He asks:

> **“How does the teacher demonstrate the conclusion from the Word?”**

He does not begin with:

> “What does my experience tell me?”

He asks:

> **“What does Scripture establish, and how should my experience be evaluated in its light?”**

The authority relationship has now become operational.

---

## 85.80 The Foundation School Is Not a Rival to the Graphē

The Foundation School exists to teach the Six First Principles.

It does not replace Scripture.

Its textbook does not replace Scripture.

Its courses do not replace Scripture.

Its exercises do not replace Scripture.

Its teachers do not replace Scripture.

Its assessments do not replace Scripture.

Its certificates do not replace Scripture.

The school is a learning environment.

The Graphē remains the governing written authority.

---

## 85.81 The Six Principles Are Not a Rival to the Graphē

The reverse must also be stated.

The Six First Principles are not an alternative to the Graphē.

They are foundational doctrines identified from the Graphē.

The learner does not choose between:

> **Graphē**

and

> **Six First Principles.**

He moves from:

> **Graphē**

to:

> **understanding what the Graphē teaches concerning the Six First Principles.**

That is the correct relationship.

---

## 85.82 The Difference Between Authority and Content

This distinction can be reduced to two questions.

### Authority

> **What governs the determination of truth?**

The answer in the architecture of this book is the authoritative written Word.

### Content

> **What foundational doctrines are to be studied?**

Hebrews 6:1–2 identifies the Six First Principles.

Authority and content are related.

They are not interchangeable.

The Doctrine of the Graphē concerns the first.

The Foundation School develops the second.

---

## 85.83 The Difference Between Gate and Curriculum

A gate answers:

> **How do you enter?**

A curriculum answers:

> **What do you study once you have entered?**

The Doctrine of the Graphē answers the first question.

The Six First Principles answer the second.

This is why the Graphē should not be counted as a seventh principle.

It performs a different function.

---

## 85.84 The Difference Between Preparation and Progression

Preparation is not the same as progression.

This book has prepared the learner.

The Six First Principles provide the next progression.

The learner should therefore not remain indefinitely in preparation.

At some point, preparation must become study.

Study must become exercise.

Exercise must become skill.

Skill must become maturity.

Maturity must become responsible service.

The gate exists to lead forward.

---

## 85.85 The Difference Between Knowing the Gate and Entering

A person can study the Doctrine of the Graphē and still fail to study the Word.

That would be an irony.

The book would have become an object of intellectual fascination instead of a preparation for faithful engagement.

The correct result is movement.

The learner should leave this work with greater appetite for the Word.

Greater respect for the Word.

Greater responsibility toward the Word.

Greater skill in handling the Word.

And readiness to study what the Word teaches next.

---

## 85.86 The Book Must Create Curiosity, Not Dependency

The conclusion of the manuscript should therefore create curiosity.

The reader should see that the field beyond this gate is substantial.

The Six First Principles are not slogans.

Each opens a serious field of study.

The reader should want to examine them.

But the book should not make the reader dependent upon itself for that examination.

It should send the learner to the next study with a better method and a better relationship to the source.

That is successful completion.

---

## 85.87 The Scholar Becomes the Student Again

The approved workman remains a learner.

The mature learner remains teachable.

The scholar remains accountable.

The person who has studied eighty-five chapters does not graduate from correction.

He becomes more responsible for correction.

He should be able to say:

> “Show me the text.”

> “Show me the reasoning.”

> “Show me the evidence.”

> “Show me where I am wrong.”

This is not insecurity.

It is scholarly integrity.

---

## 85.88 The Foundation Is Entered With Humility

The Six First Principles should therefore be entered with humility.

The learner knows that the first principles are foundational.

He also knows that his understanding of them can be incomplete.

He should not confuse familiarity with mastery.

He should not confuse vocabulary with understanding.

He should not confuse repetition with skill.

He should not confuse confidence with truth.

He should labour.

---

## 85.89 The Foundation Is Entered With Confidence in the Source

Humility toward one's interpretation does not require uncertainty about the authority of the source.

The learner can be humble about himself while being confident in the Word.

That distinction is important.

The posture is:

> **confidence in the authority of the Graphē; humility concerning my handling of it.**

This is a mature scholarly posture.

---

## 85.90 The Foundation Is Entered With Responsibility

The learner also understands that increased knowledge increases responsibility.

The more he learns, the more carefully he must handle what he has learned.

If he becomes a teacher, he carries greater responsibility.

If he becomes a workman, he must labour faithfully.

If he discovers an error in his interpretation, he must correct it.

The gate therefore leads not merely to information but to responsibility.

---

## 85.91 The Six Principles and the Future Teacher

Hebrews 5:12 speaks of those who ought to be teachers.

The movement toward the Six First Principles therefore belongs within a larger developmental architecture.

The learner is not being trained merely to pass an examination.

He is being prepared for greater capacity.

The study of foundational doctrine should eventually produce people capable of teaching foundational doctrine faithfully.

That requires more than memorization.

It requires understanding, reasoning, discernment, and right handling.

---

## 85.92 The Gate and the Teacher's Responsibility

The teacher of the Six First Principles therefore carries the same obligation established in Chapter 83.

He is a workman.

He must be diligent.

He must rightly handle the Word.

He must distinguish source from interpretation.

He must avoid doctrinal inflation.

He must be correctable.

He must not make students dependent upon his personality.

He must direct them toward the Graphē.

The gate remains active even after the student enters.

---

## 85.93 The Gate and the Student's Responsibility

The student carries responsibility as well.

He should not say:

> “My teacher said it.”

and consider the matter finished.

He should learn to examine.

He should learn to ask.

He should learn to compare.

He should learn to reason.

He should learn to write.

He should learn to defend a conclusion.

He should learn to revise a conclusion.

The student becomes a participant in the work.

---

## 85.94 The Six Principles Must Be Handled, Not Merely Repeated

This returns the reader to the central theme of Movement X.

The scholarly labour of Scripture is not satisfied by repetition.

A learner may repeat:

> repentance,

> faith,

> baptisms,

> laying on of hands,

> resurrection,

> judgment,

without understanding any of them deeply.

The goal is not verbal possession.

It is trained understanding.

The learner must handle the content.

---

## 85.95 The Graphē-to-Principles Sequence

The entire relationship can now be condensed:

> **Graphē**
>
> **→ Authority**
>
> **→ Perception**
>
> **→ Learning**
>
> **→ Understanding**
>
> **→ Reasoning**
>
> **→ Diligence**
>
> **→ Exercise**
>
> **→ Skill**
>
> **→ Maturity**
>
> **→ Right Handling**
>
> **→ Readiness**
>
> **→ Six First Principles**

This is not a new seven-part doctrinal list.

It is a developmental and architectural sequence.

---

## 85.96 The Six Remain the Six

Therefore the decisive conclusion is:

> **The Doctrine of the Graphē does not add a seventh first principle.**

The Six First Principles remain:

> **Repentance from Dead Works**

> **Faith Toward God**

> **The Doctrine of Baptisms**

> **Laying on of Hands**

> **Resurrection of the Dead**

> **Eternal Judgment**

The Graphē stands before them as the authoritative written foundation and gate through which they are to be entered, studied, interpreted, and handled.

Nothing has been added to Hebrews.

Nothing has been removed from Hebrews.

The architecture has been clarified.

---

## 85.97 Why the Gate Must Come First

The reason the gate comes first can now be stated in one sentence:

> **The learner must know how the authoritative written Word governs doctrinal study before he is entrusted with the responsibility of handling foundational doctrine.**

That is why this book precedes the Six First Principles.

Not because the Graphē is a seventh doctrine.

Not because the Graphē is one of the six.

But because the Graphē establishes the authority relationship within which the six are to be studied.

---

## 85.98 The Book's Final Intellectual Achievement

The achievement of *One Source of Truth* is therefore not that it has replaced the learner's need to study Scripture.

It has established the opposite.

It has shown why the learner must study Scripture seriously.

It has shown why the learner must distinguish source from interpretation.

It has shown why reasoning is necessary.

It has shown why diligence is necessary.

It has shown why exercise is necessary.

It has shown why maturity is necessary.

It has shown why right handling is necessary.

And it has brought the learner to the point where those disciplines can be applied to the foundational doctrine that comes next.

---

## 85.99 The Book's Final Practical Charge

The learner should therefore leave this book with a simple charge:

> **Do not merely possess the Word.**

> **Know it.**

> **Understand it.**

> **Reason through it.**

> **Exercise it.**

> **Handle it rightly.**

> **Remain correctable.**

> **And enter the Six First Principles under its authority.**

This is the practical completion of the scholarly labour.

---

## 85.100 The Foundation Is Not to Be Laid Again Forever

Hebrews warns against remaining permanently at the stage where the foundation must continually be laid again.

The learner must therefore move.

There is a time to establish.

There is a time to exercise.

There is a time to mature.

There is a time to teach.

The present book has established the gate.

The next field requires entry.

The learner should not confuse preparation with perpetual preparation.

---

## 85.101 Going On

Hebrews 6:1 says:

> **“Let us go on unto perfection.”**

The movement is forward.

The learner carries the foundation.

He does not abandon it.

He does not worship it as an end in itself.

He builds upon it.

The Doctrine of the Graphē therefore does not terminate the learner's study.

It sends him forward.

---

## 85.102 What the Graphē Gives the Learner

The Doctrine of the Graphē gives the learner at least six essential disciplines for the next stage.

### First — Authority

He knows where primary written authority belongs.

### Second — Distinction

He can distinguish Scripture from interpretation.

### Third — Reasoning

He can follow arguments rather than merely collect verses.

### Fourth — Responsibility

He understands that handling the Word is accountable work.

### Fifth — Correction

He knows that his interpretation can be wrong.

### Sixth — Readiness

He is prepared to enter foundational doctrine with intellectual discipline.

These are not six new principles.

They are fruits of the gate.

---

## 85.103 What the Graphē Does Not Give the Learner

The Doctrine of the Graphē does not make the learner automatically knowledgeable in every doctrinal field.

It does not mean that he has mastered repentance.

It does not mean that he has mastered faith.

It does not mean that he has mastered baptisms.

It does not mean that he has mastered laying on of hands.

It does not mean that he has mastered resurrection.

It does not mean that he has mastered eternal judgment.

Those fields still require study.

The gate prepares.

The curriculum teaches.

The learner labours.

---

## 85.104 The Boundary Must Remain Visible

A rigorous architecture keeps its boundaries visible.

Therefore:

> **Doctrine of the Graphē**

is not:

> **Repentance from Dead Works.**

It is not:

> **Faith Toward God.**

It is not:

> **The Doctrine of Baptisms.**

It is not:

> **Laying on of Hands.**

It is not:

> **Resurrection of the Dead.**

It is not:

> **Eternal Judgment.**

It establishes the authority framework for studying all six.

---

## 85.105 The Graphē as Foundation/Gate

The final structural statement can now be written:

> **One Source of Truth — The Doctrine of the Graphē**
>
> **is the foundational work and entrance gate into the Six First Principles.**

It establishes the learner's relationship to Holy Writ.

It develops the scholarly capacity required to handle Holy Writ.

It establishes the discipline by which the learner should approach foundational doctrine.

It does not become another first principle.

That is the architecture.

---

## 85.106 The Graphē and the Six First Principles in One View

The relationship is:

> **THE GRAPHĒ**
>
> *authoritative written Word*
>
> ↓
>
> **THE DOCTRINE OF THE GRAPHĒ**
>
> *authority, nature, authentication, handling, interpretation, scholarly discipline*
>
> ↓
>
> **READINESS**
>
> *diligence, skill, maturity, right handling*
>
> ↓
>
> **THE SIX FIRST PRINCIPLES**
>
> 1. *Repentance from Dead Works*
>
> 2. *Faith Toward God*
>
> 3. *The Doctrine of Baptisms*
>
> 4. *Laying on of Hands*
>
> 5. *Resurrection of the Dead*
>
> 6. *Eternal Judgment*
>
> ↓
>
> **MATURITY AND FURTHER DEVELOPMENT**

The Doctrine of the Graphē is therefore a gate between the learner and the foundational doctrinal curriculum.

---

## 85.107 The Final Anti-Circularity Check

The final argument must not become circular.

We are not saying:

> “The Graphē is the foundation because the Graphē says it is the foundation.”

The present conclusion depends upon the cumulative work of the manuscript.

The book has investigated truth.

It has examined evidence.

It has considered the ground of truth.

It has developed the argument concerning God.

It has examined revelation.

It has considered the written record.

It has treated authentication, authority, Christ, Scripture, interpretation, and right handling.

Within that established architecture, the learner is now shown the proper function of the Graphē in relation to the Six First Principles.

The conclusion is architectural.

It is not a circular assertion.

---

## 85.108 The Final Source-Authority Check

Nor should the reader conclude:

> “The book is now finished, therefore the book is authoritative.”

The book is finished as a manuscript project.

That does not transform it into Scripture.

The distinction remains.

The reader must continue to examine the claims made here.

The Graphē remains primary.

The book remains secondary.

The teacher remains secondary.

The course remains secondary.

The institution remains secondary.

This hierarchy is part of the conclusion itself.

---

## 85.109 The Final Interpretation Check

The same discipline applies to the present chapter.

The reader should distinguish:

> what Hebrews explicitly names;

from:

> what this chapter reasons about the architectural relationship;

from:

> what the educational system does with that relationship.

Hebrews names the first principles.

The manuscript explains why the Doctrine of the Graphē should function as their gate.

The curriculum operationalizes the study.

These are related levels.

They must not be conflated.

---

## 85.110 The Final Readiness Check

The learner is ready for the next stage if he can answer:

1. What is the Graphē?
2. Why is the written Word authoritative within the architecture of this work?
3. Why must interpretation remain subordinate to the source?
4. Why must the learner distinguish quotation, interpretation, inference, and application?
5. Why is diligence required?
6. Why does exercise produce skill?
7. Why does maturity involve trained discernment?
8. What does it mean to rightly handle the Word?
9. What does it mean to be an approved workman?
10. Why does the Doctrine of the Graphē come before the Six First Principles?
11. What are the Six First Principles?
12. Why is the Doctrine of the Graphē not a seventh principle?

If these questions can be answered with reasons rather than slogans, the gate has served its purpose.

---

## 85.111 The Six First Principles Remain Ahead

The reader should therefore resist the temptation to close the book by saying:

> “I have finished the doctrine.”

No.

The present investigation has reached its assigned conclusion.

A new field now stands ahead.

The Six First Principles require their own study.

Their meaning, biblical grounding, distinctions, implications, and applications must be worked through.

That work belongs to the next stage.

---

## 85.112 The Book Ends by Sending the Learner Back to the Word

The strongest ending is therefore not:

> “Believe this book.”

It is:

> **“Now go to the Word.”**

Take the discipline with you.

Take the questions with you.

Take the humility with you.

Take the diligence with you.

Take the skill with you.

Take the willingness to be corrected with you.

And enter the foundational doctrine under the authority of the Graphē.

---

## 85.113 The Final Relationship

The relationship can now be stated one final time:

> **The Graphē is the source.**

> **The Doctrine of the Graphē establishes the learner's relationship to that source.**

> **The scholarly discipline teaches the learner how to engage that source responsibly.**

> **The Six First Principles are the foundational doctrinal field into which the prepared learner now proceeds.**

Therefore:

> **The Doctrine of the Graphē is the foundation/gate, not a seventh first principle.**

---

## 85.114 From Source to Foundation

The title of this final chapter is therefore deliberate:

> **From Graphē to the Six First Principles.**

Not:

> Graphē plus six equals seven.

Not:

> Graphē replaces the six.

Not:

> Graphē becomes the first of seven.

Rather:

> **Graphē → gate → Six First Principles.**

The movement is from authoritative written source to prepared doctrinal study.

---

## 85.115 The Final Charge to the Workman

The workman now stands before the foundation.

He has been told to be diligent.

He has been taught to exercise.

He has been warned against unskillfulness.

He has been taught to rightly divide.

He has been shown the responsibility of approval.

He has been given a discipline of interpretation.

He has been reminded that his conclusions remain corrigible.

Now he must work.

Not merely talk about Scripture.

Not merely quote Scripture.

Not merely defend Scripture.

Not merely possess Scripture.

He must handle it.

---

## 85.116 The Final Charge to the Learner

Therefore the learner should proceed with four commitments:

> **Read faithfully.**

> **Reason honestly.**

> **Handle carefully.**

> **Obey what the Word establishes.**

These commitments belong to every stage that follows.

---

## 85.117 The Final Charge to the Teacher

And the teacher should proceed with four corresponding responsibilities:

> **Teach from the source.**

> **Expose the reasoning.**

> **Distinguish interpretation from Scripture.**

> **Develop learners who can work responsibly without perpetual dependence.**

That is the continuation of approved workmanship.

---

## 85.118 The Final Charge to the School

And the school should function accordingly.

Its curriculum should direct the learner to the Word.

Its courses should teach the Six First Principles.

Its exercises should develop skill.

Its teachers should remain servants.

Its assessments should measure demonstrated understanding.

Its structure should preserve the six principles as six.

Its gate should remain the Doctrine of the Graphē.

---

## 85.119 The Final Architectural Formula

The entire relationship can therefore be expressed as:

> **SOURCE**
>
> **Graphē**
>
> ↓
>
> **GATE**
>
> **Doctrine of the Graphē**
>
> ↓
>
> **READINESS**
>
> **Diligence · Exercise · Skill · Maturity · Right Handling**
>
> ↓
>
> **FOUNDATION**
>
> **The Six First Principles**
>
> ↓
>
> **PROGRESSION**
>
> **Further maturity, understanding, and faithful service**

This is the architecture the manuscript has been building toward.

---

## 85.120 The Final Conclusion

The Doctrine of the Graphē does not stand beside the Six First Principles as another principle.

It stands before them.

It establishes the learner's relationship to the authoritative written Word.

It teaches why the Word must be taken seriously.

It develops the intellectual discipline required to perceive, understand, reason through, compare, distinguish, infer, test, conclude, and apply what is written.

It trains the workman to remain accountable.

It prepares the learner for foundational doctrine.

And then it yields the stage.

The Six First Principles remain the Six First Principles named in Hebrews 6:1–2:

> **Repentance from Dead Works.**

> **Faith Toward God.**

> **The Doctrine of Baptisms.**

> **Laying on of Hands.**

> **Resurrection of the Dead.**

> **Eternal Judgment.**

The Doctrine of the Graphē is not the seventh.

It is the gate.

The book therefore does not end by adding another principle.

It ends by opening the way to the principles already given.

And the prepared learner now stands where Hebrews calls him to stand:

> **“Let us go on unto perfection.”**

The foundation has been established.

The workman has been prepared.

The source remains the authority.

The next work is to enter, study, exercise, and build.

> **From Graphē to the Six First Principles.**

chapters.title: The First Principles of the Oracles of God
chapters.body:
This book is not a second Bible. Holy Scripture is the authority. What follows opens the first principles of the oracles of God, unto maturity.

The cover of this volume may say Truth · Knowledge · Maturity. That line belongs to this book. The house that holds the book is Aletheia: Truth · Identity · Dominion. Do not confuse the two.

The full treatment of this written authority is the standalone book One Source of Truth: The Doctrine of the Graphē. This chapter remains the school opening into the six first principles. It does not invent a seventh course. It does not replace Holy Writ as the written authority.

A student at three hours a week must have something to sit with. An intensive student uses the same text with longer writing. The doctrine does not change with the clock.

I. THE GRAPHĒ

A. The design of God

Over the ages the design of God for a Christian experience — following the teachings, or manifesting the qualities or spirit, of Jesus Christ — has rested in conformity with the unleavened sincerity and truth of the graphē: Holy Writ, the Bible, Scripture.

This school calls that experience Scripture-conforming. The word names an experience that follows the teachings of Jesus Christ, manifests His qualities or His spirit, and remains under the authority of the graphē. The experience rests under the writing. It does not invent a likeness and then hunt for a verse to bless it.

Graphē is Holy Writ: the Bible, Scripture. It is writings or sayings of unchallenged, unquestionable authority. That is the term. Keep it there. Do not turn it into a theory of inspiration you were not asked to invent.

B. John 10:34-36 with Psalm 82:6

The Lord Jesus answered a charge of blasphemy by appeal to that which was written. He would not let men set His word against the writing.

John 10:34 — “Jesus answered them, Is it not written in your law, I said, Ye are gods?”

John 10:35 — “If he called them gods, unto whom the word of God came, and the scripture cannot be broken;”

John 10:36 — “Say ye of him, whom the Father hath sanctified, and sent into the world, Thou blasphemest; because I said, I am the Son of God?”

The writing He cited is Psalm 82:6 — “I have said, Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High.”

Who speaks in John 10? The Lord Jesus. To whom? Jews who had taken up stones because He said, I and my Father are one. Why? Because they charged blasphemy, and He answered from the writing they already owned as law.

Hold the Scripture set. He does not argue from mood. He does not argue from a private voice. He argues from what is written. He names the persons in the psalm as those unto whom the word of God came. Then He sets the rule that governs this school: the scripture cannot be broken.

Psalm 82:7 remains in the psalm: “But ye shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes.” Chapter 3 will open image and likeness with that verse still in the teaching. Here the point is narrower. The Lord treats the writing as unbreakable even when men use it against Him. If He will not break it, you will not be asked to break it to make a convenient Christian experience.

C. The authority of Holy Writ

Holy Writ is writings or sayings of unchallenged, unquestionable authority. That authority governs persons, organizations, governments, and nations.

This authority is not a church stamp on a dust jacket. It is the authority of the writing itself. Persons are under it. Organizations that appear Christianized are under it. Governments are under it. Nations are under it. Age does not exempt. Size does not exempt. A meeting that calls itself a school does not exempt.

If you will hear from God in this year, you will hear Him where He has spoken. You will not be asked to invent a more convenient Bible.

D. Substitute religious likenesses

There is another thing that calls itself Christian experience and is not. It is a substitute religious likeness: language and appearance that resemble the faith while refusing to sit under the text.

A substitute may borrow biblical sound, Christian vocabulary, and religious appearance. It becomes false when it refuses to let the words of Scripture mean what they say. What remains is religious imitation after the graphē is no longer allowed to govern.

This school will not trade the graphē for that likeness. A man may be sincere in the likeness. Sincerity does not make the likeness the writing. An organization may be old in the likeness. Age does not make the likeness the oracles of God.

The distinction is not “Bible people” versus “unspiritual people.” The distinction is conformity with the unleavened sincerity and truth of the graphē versus a religious substitute that uses Bible words as decoration. Unleavened sincerity is not a mood of honesty. It is the refusal to mix the writing with a substitute and call the mixture experience.

E. Principle, reasoning, application, charge

Principle: the Christian experience this school teaches rests under the graphē. The writing cannot be broken. The authority of Holy Writ governs you.

Reasoning: if the Lord answers a charge of blasphemy from the writing, you do not rise above the writing to answer a charge of dullness. If the writing governs nations, it governs your week. If a likeness will not sit down under the text, it is not the experience this school names.

Application: you will read this year with the text open. You will not treat a slogan, a house line, or a cover line as if it were Scripture. You will not treat this textbook as a second Bible. When a verse is taught, you will have the verse.

Charge: write one page. Where have you treated a likeness of the faith as if it were the graphē? Name the likeness. Name the verse you used to bless it. Then name the verse you will continue in this week, written in full, and say what it says — not what you wish it said.

II. THE WRITTEN AUTHORITY

A. The graphē is the appointed written authority

The graphē — Holy Writ, the Bible, Scripture — is the appointed written authority for hearing from God and for spiritual growth. It is first in order because God has bound His speaking to the writing He gave. It is not a conference, not a brand, not this handbook, and not this course.

Over the ages the design of God for a Scripture-conforming Christian experience has rested under the unleavened sincerity and truth of that writing. If you will hear, you hear where He has spoken. If you will grow, you grow under that writing — first principles, then maturity.

B. The essential cornerstone

This book opens the essential cornerstone of Christianity: the first principles of the oracles of God. It opens the foundation; it does not take the place of the graphē.

Hebrews 5:12 — “For when for the time ye ought to be teachers, ye have need that one teach you again which be the first principles of the oracles of God; and are become such as have need of milk, and not of strong meat.”

The verse will be opened in section III. The first principles of the oracles of God are the cornerstone. A cornerstone is not an ornament. It is what the house is set on. If it is not laid, the house is not the house the writer of Hebrews is building.

Oracles of God are not private impressions. They are the speaking of God already bound in the graphē, and the first principles of that speaking are named in Hebrews 6:1-2. This chapter is the gate into those six. It is not itself a seventh.

C. Two movements, not one slogan

Under the written authority, growth is two movements, not one slogan:

1. First principles.
2. Maturity — perfection.

You do not skip the foundation to appear mature. You do not relay the foundation every year as a lifestyle and call that growth.

Hebrews 6:1 — “Therefore leaving the principles of the doctrine of Christ, let us go on unto perfection; not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works, and of faith toward God,”

Leaving them does not mean forgetting them. It means they are laid, and you go on. A man who has never laid them is not “leaving” them. He is skipping them. A man who lays them every year as a habit of indecision is not going on. He is relaying what ought already to bear weight.

Perfection is maturity: the second movement. It is not a claim that you have finished God. It is the writer’s word for going on once the foundation is down. Hebrews 6:3 will bind that going-on to permission. Do not treat maturity as a human schedule you can force.

D. Hearing from God

Hearing from God and spiritual growth are not two religions. You hear where He has spoken — in the graphē. You grow as the first principles are laid and you go on. A people who will not sit under the writing will not hear by inventing a louder room. A people who skip the six will not mature by collecting meat they cannot digest.

This school exists because the oracles have a beginning that must be known, distinguished, reasoned, and taught. The year is fifty-two weeks. Course 1 occupies the first nine. The remaining courses occupy the rest, in the order Hebrews names the stones. You will not be given a seventh Year-1 course to make the year feel fuller.

E. Charge

Write six lines. What have you called “growth” that was only a relaying of an unlaid foundation? What have you called “maturity” that was a skip? Then write Hebrews 6:1 in your own hand and mark the two verbs: leaving, go on. You cannot do the second honestly until the first has a foundation under it.

III. HEBREWS 5:11–12 — YOU OUGHT TO BE TEACHERS

A. Dull of hearing

Hebrews 5:11 — “Of whom we have many things to say, and hard to be uttered, seeing ye are dull of hearing.”

Of whom? The writer has been speaking of Melchisedec and of the Son, a priest for ever after that order. He has many things to say. They are hard to be uttered. The hardness is not in the doctrine as if the truth were unclear. The hardness is in the ear.

To whom does he write? A people who have had the word long enough that time itself has become an argument against them. Why? Because they have become dull of hearing, and the meat concerning the Son cannot be given to an ear that will not take it.

Dull of hearing is the first mark of the babe. It will return in section V. Here you must see it as the reason meat is withheld. The writer is not teasing them. He is diagnosing them. A school that withholds meat because the ear is dull is not being cruel. It is being Hebrews.

B. For the time ye ought to be teachers

Hebrews 5:12 — “For when for the time ye ought to be teachers, ye have need that one teach you again which be the first principles of the oracles of God; and are become such as have need of milk, and not of strong meat.”

Mark the time. They had been under the word long enough that they ought to be teachers. Ought is obligation, not compliment. Time had done its part. They had not.

They have need that one teach them again. Again is the wound. The first principles are not new to them as a rumour. They are new to them again because they were not kept. A man can sit under oracles and lose the beginning.

They are become such as have need of milk, and not of strong meat. Become is a direction. A people can recede. Milk is not an insult to a newborn. Milk is an indictment to a man who has had years to grow.

C. Milk and strong meat

Milk is the diet of the babe. Strong meat is the diet of those of full age. The first principles are not a lesser gospel. They are the foundation that makes meat possible.

Do not despise milk as if the six were childish slogans. A newborn must have milk. Do not demand milk as a lifestyle after the time you ought to be a teacher. The same food that saves a child accuses a man who will not grow.

Strong meat is not a different Bible. It is the same graphē taken by senses that have been exercised. Hebrews 5:14 will name those senses. You will not reach 5:14 by skipping 5:12.

If you cannot teach repentance from dead works from the Scriptures, you are not ready to speak as if you were past it. That is not a slight on your zeal. It is the writer’s order. This school will not give you Chapter 7 language to hide an unlaid first stone.

D. Scripture set, distinction, principle

Hold 5:11 and 5:12 together. Dull hearing is why the hard things cannot be uttered. Time is why they ought to be teachers. Again is why the first principles must be taught. Become is why a people can need milk after years.

Distinction: milk as kindness to a newborn versus milk as indictment to a man who has had time. First principles as foundation versus first principles as a lesser gospel you outgrow by forgetting.

Principle: there is a time when you ought to be teachers. After that time, need of milk is recession, not humility.

Reasoning: if the fault were in the doctrine, the writer would have less to say. He has many things to say. If the fault were lack of meetings, time would have cured it. Time has already passed. The fault is in the ear and in the failure to keep the beginning.

Application: name the time you have already had. Do not write “a long time.” Write the years, or the seasons, or the books you have already handled. Then ask whether you can teach the first principles, or only repeat their names.

Charge: where are you still a hearer who must be taught the oracles again? Write Hebrews 5:12 in your own hand. Reason “ought,” “again,” and “become.” Do not recite the verse as if recitation were skill.

IV. APEIROS — UNSKILFUL IN THE WORD OF RIGHTEOUSNESS

A. The verse and the term

Hebrews 5:13 — “For every one that useth milk is unskilful in the word of righteousness: for he is a babe.”

Unskilful is Greek ἄπειρος (apeiros, G552): inexperienced, that is, ignorant — unskilful. This teaching keeps the word there. The inexperience is not in crowding a meeting. It is in the word of righteousness.

ἄπειρος (apeiros) is not a personality type. It is not shyness. It is not lack of a platform. It is lack of experience in the word that names righteousness — the writing in which a man is shown what is right before God and what is not. A man may be experienced in rooms and ἄπειρος (apeiros) in that word.

B. Hebrews 5:14 in the same Scripture set

Hebrews 5:14 — “But strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil.”

Hold 5:13 and 5:14. The milk-user is ἄπειρος (apeiros) and a babe. The one of full age has senses exercised by reason of use. Use is not attendance. Use is the labour that trains hearing to discern.

Discern both good and evil. The babe is not merely under-informed. He cannot yet distinguish. That is why unskilfulness produces, in this severity, damnable accepted heresies called doctrines. A people who cannot discern will baptize error and call it teaching.

C. Dryness and doctrinal turning aside

This teaching is plain: when sound judgment is absent and unskillfulness remains, spiritual dryness and doctrinal turning aside appear among persons and even among age-old organizations that appear Christianized. What follows can be damnable heresies accepted and called doctrines.

Sound judgment is not a polite temperament. It is the capacity to hold the writing and judge under it. Absence of that judgment, together with ἄπειρος (apeiros), dries a people. This dryness is not a mood in a room; it is the failure to yield what the oracles planted.

Doctrinal turning aside is desertion of a position: turning, shifting, refusing to stay under what was said. A person can do it. An age-old organization that appears Christianized can do it. Appearance is not skill. Years on a signboard are not senses exercised.

What follows that dryness and that turning is not a harmless confusion. This teaching names the fruit: damnable accepted heresies called doctrines. Accepted means the heresy has become the house diet. Called doctrines means the name “doctrine” has been put on what the graphē will not bear. This school will not soften that sentence.

D. Scripture’s demand for diligent study

That lack of skill is blamed on failure to receive Scripture’s demand for diligent study and to align accordingly: failure to know the Scriptures, whether held digitally or in print.

This demand for diligent study is not a degree. It is the push the writing itself gives toward knowing — toward labour in the text. A digital copy or a physical copy does not matter if there is no labour. A glowing screen can hide ἄπειρος (apeiros) as easily as a closed book.

The cure is not a louder room. The cure is labour in the word. Section VI will name that labour σπουδάζω (spoudazō). Do not wait for section VI to begin it. If you cannot name the hour and the text of this week, you are already answering Hebrews 5:13.

E. Distinction, principle, charge

Distinction: skill in the word of righteousness versus performance in a crowded room. Inexperience in the writing versus inexperience in platform. Sound judgment versus accepted heresy called doctrine.

Principle: every one that useth milk is ἄπειρος (apeiros) in the word of righteousness. The inexperience is in the writing. Organizations can be ἄπειρος (apeiros). The cure is to know the Scriptures and align.

Reasoning: if unskilfulness were lack of activity, busy houses would be mature. This teaching watches age-old organizations dry up. If the copy format were the issue, the hard book would have saved the last century. The issue is failure to know and to align.

Application: what is your actual study labour this week? Name the hour. Name the text. If you cannot name it, you are not yet a workman. You may be a hearer. Hebrews has already told you what a hearer can become after time.

Charge: write Hebrews 5:13-14. Then write six sentences that do not repeat the heading: what ἄπειρος (apeiros) is, what it is not, what spiritual dryness looks like in a person, what doctrinal turning aside looks like in a house, what “accepted heresies called doctrines” forces you to refuse, and what labour you will put on the word of righteousness before the week ends.

V. NĒPIOS — TWO MARKS OF BABES

A. The term

The same verse names the milk-user a babe: Greek νήπιος (nēpios, G3516) — implying negation; figuratively a simple-minded person, an immature Christian: babe, child.

This teaching will not let you take “babe” as a term of endearment here. It is a diagnosis. A babe may be sincere and still be ἄπειρος (apeiros). An organization may be old and still be νήπιος (nēpios). Anyone — person or organization — unskilled in the word of righteousness is a νήπιος (nēpios).

Simple-minded, here, is not an insult to the poor in spirit. It is the mind that has not been exercised to discern. Immature Christian is not “young in years.” It is behind the time you ought to have been a teacher.

B. Two characteristics

Two characteristics of babes:

1. Dull of hearing (Hebrews 5:11).
2. Unskilled in the Word, which is the basis for salvation.

The first mark is the ear. The second is the skill. They are not one mark said twice. A man may hear much and remain unskilled. A man may handle words and remain dull. Hebrews names both.

The Word is the basis for salvation. If you are unskilled there, you are unskilled at the root. This is not a side comment about study habits. Salvation itself sits on that Word. Unskill in the word of righteousness is unskill at the place a man is saved, kept, and grown.

Do not invent a third mark to make the list feel complete. There are two. Dull of hearing. Unskilled in the Word. Hold them until you can name them in your sleep and apply them to a person and to a house without cruelty and without flattery.

C. Babe versus teacher

Hebrews 5:14 has already named the other pole: them that are of full age, who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil.

The distinction is not teacher as office versus babe as pew. The writer said they ought to be teachers. The obligation is that the first principles can be taught by those who have had time. A man who cannot teach repentance from dead works from the Scriptures is not yet past milk, whatever title he carries.

A babe may love God and still be νήπιος (nēpios). Love does not cancel the diagnosis. An organization may print Bible verses on its walls and still be νήπιος (nēpios). Print does not cancel ἄπειρος (apeiros).

D. Why this piece was written

This teaching states the aim of the piece: that you may experience productive living, be in control, and experience godliness in all capacities — not by a slogan, but by skill in the word of righteousness.

Productive living is not a prosperity motto. It is a life that yields what the oracles planted. In control is not a technique for managing rooms. It is a man no longer driven by the dullness and the unskill that produce spiritual dryness. Godliness in all capacities is not a brand of manners. It is the life the graphē governs in every capacity you actually have — person, house, labour, and nation under the authority already named.

You will not reach that aim by collecting quotations. You will not reach it by remaining a babe and calling the remaining humility. You will reach it, if you reach it, by the labour section VI names, under the permission section X names.

E. Charge

Name your dullness of hearing. Name where you are ἄπειρος (apeiros) in the word of righteousness. Do not write a general confession. Write the place. Then write the two marks as you would teach them to a babe, and as you would stand behind them before a teacher. If you cannot do both, you are still in 5:12.

VI. SPOUDAZŌ — STUDY AS LABOUR

A. The verse

2 Timothy 2:15 — “Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.”

Who writes? Paul. To whom? Timothy, a man already entrusted with the word, told to endure hardness as a good soldier, and not to be ashamed of the testimony. Why? Because the word of truth must be handled by a workman, and approval here is not a feeling in a meeting. It is the approval of God toward a man who has laboured so as not to be ashamed of the work.

2 Timothy 2:3 — “Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ.”

2 Timothy 2:8 — “Remember that Jesus Christ of the seed of David was raised from the dead according to my gospel:”

2 Timothy 2:9 — “Wherein I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound.”

Hold the Scripture set. Study sits in a letter about hardness, shame, and a word that is not bound. Spoudazō is not a hobby for quiet evenings. It is labour in a war where the word must be divided rightly and the workman must not blush before God.

B. The term

The Greek behind that study is σπουδάζω (spoudazō, G4704): to use speed, to make effort, be prompt or earnest; do diligence, be diligent, endeavour, labour, study — intellectually.

Speed here is not haste that skips context. It is earnestness that will not postpone the labour. Effort is not noise. Promptness is not a calendar app. Earnestness is the refusal to treat the oracles as optional once the week fills. Diligence, endeavour, labour, study: the English is stacked so you cannot reduce the word to “read a verse if you feel like it.”

Intellectually is part of the definition. This school will not despise the mind as if reasoning were unbelief. Knowledge, in the next section, is perception and learning and reasoning. Spoudazō is the labour that makes that knowledge possible.

C. Approved, workman, rightly dividing

Walk the verse. Do not slogan it.

Study: the imperative. You are commanded to this labour. You are not invited to admire it.

To shew thyself: the labour is visible in the work, not in the claim. You shew yourself by the workmanship.

Approved unto God: the audience of the approval is God. Men may approve a crowded room. This verse does not ask that room for a stamp.

A workman: approval here is the approval of a workman. The work is the word of truth. A workman has a craft. He can be ashamed if the craft is slovenly. He needeth not to be ashamed when the word is rightly divided.

That needeth not to be ashamed: shame in this verse is the shame of bad work before God, not social embarrassment. A man can be loud and ashamed in this sense. A man can be quiet and unashamed.

Rightly dividing the word of truth: the word is truth. It can be divided wrongly. Dull hearing and ἄπειρος (apeiros) produce the wrong division. Right division holds a Scripture set, keeps a distinction, and will not merge what the text keeps apart. This year will ask you to divide the six principles and not invent a seventh. It will ask you to divide metanoia from μεταμέλομαι (metamellomai). It will ask you to divide two old things. If you cannot divide, you are not yet this workman.

D. Three hours and eight

If you will walk this year at three hours a week or at eight, the difference is not a second doctrine. The difference is how much labour you put on the same oracles.

The Walk: about three hours a week, fifty-two weeks, the same six courses. Intensive: about eight hours a week, fifty-two weeks, the same six courses. Same examinations. Same certificate when a certificate is issued. No second curriculum.

Three hours will not excuse you from σπουδάζω (spoudazō). Eight hours will not create a different gospel. The Intensive student writes longer, drills more, and sits longer with the same Scripture set. The Walk student writes tighter on the same Scripture set. Both must reason. Neither may hide in quotation.

E. Charge — word drill on the verse

Do a word drill on 2 Timothy 2:15 until you can reason “approved,” “workman,” and “rightly dividing” without a slogan.

Write the verse in your own hand.

Write what approved means in this verse — unto whom, for what kind of person.

Write what workman means — what the work is, what shame would be.

Write what rightly dividing means — what you must not merge, what you must not skip.

Write six sentences. If you write the heading six times, you have not drilled. If you cannot do this at three hours, you will not do it at eight by wishing. Put the hour on the page.

VII. KNOWLEDGE — PERCEPTION, LEARNING, REASONING

A. The definition

Knowledge is a mental result of perception, learning, and reasoning. The practice is named: word exercise, word drill.

Knowledge, here, is not a pile of information. A man may quote a verse and still be a babe. Quotation without reasoning is not skill. Information collected is not that mental result.

Three parts, one result.

Perception: you see what the text says, not what you wish it said. You see the words in their place. You see who speaks, to whom, and why. You see the Scripture set the verse sits in. Perception is not a mystical extra. It is the refusal to skip what is on the page.

Learning: you take it in, and you keep it. You write it. You can return it. A verse you cannot write is a verse you have not yet learned, however often you have heard it. Learning is not a feeling of familiarity.

Reasoning: you can hold a Scripture set of Scriptures together and draw the distinction the text itself makes. You can say why “ought to be teachers” and “become” belong in one verse. You can say why milk is kindness in one man and indictment in another. You can say why graphē is not religious substitute. Reasoning is not speculation. It is the mind working the writing until the distinction is teachable.

B. Word exercise, word drill

The practice is not optional colour. It is how this school makes knowledge. Word exercise: you use the word, as Hebrews 5:14 said “by reason of use.” Word drill: you put the verse through perception, learning, and reasoning until you can teach it.

A drill is repetition with attention. You write the verse. You name the terms as they are used here. You set the context. You hold the Scripture set. You draw the distinction. You state the principle. You reason. You apply. You take the charge. That is the method of this book. It is not a blog outline. It is not a sermon skeleton. It is labour.

This school will ask you to reason. The questions this school asks are not decorations. They are charges. “Ye ought to be teachers” is a charge. “Study” is a charge. “Ye shall know the truth” is a charge. Later chapters will ask questions that must be answered, not waved past. You will not be allowed to treat them as rhetoric.

C. Distinction and principle

Distinction: knowledge as perception plus learning plus reasoning versus information collected versus quotation without reasoning.

Principle: you do not know a verse until you can perceive it, keep it, and reason it in its Scripture set.

Reasoning: if quotation were knowledge, the Hebrews readers would not have needed to be taught again. They had heard. If familiarity were learning, time would have made them teachers. Time had passed. If slogans were reasoning, this chapter could have been a list of headings. This teaching was already a list of headings. It was too thin to teach. You are holding the opening of that page.

Application: take Hebrews 5:12. Perceive it — what it says, not a summary. Learn it — write it. Reason it — why “ought to be teachers” and “become” belong in one verse, and what “again” does to a man who thought he had finished the beginning.

Charge: do that drill before you touch Chapter 2. Chapter 2 will not lay the first stone in a man who will not reason the gate.

VIII. TRUTH MAKES FREE

A. The verse in its place

John 8:32 — “And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.”

Read the verse in its place. Do not take it as a motto for the cover. The cover may say Truth · Knowledge · Maturity. This verse is not that line. This verse is the Lord speaking to men about remaining in His word.

John 8:31 — “Then said Jesus to those Jews which believed on him, If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed;”

John 8:32 — “And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.”

John 8:33 — “They answered him, We be Abraham's seed, and were never in bondage to any man: how sayest thou, Ye shall be made free?”

John 8:34 — “Jesus answered them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin.”

John 8:35 — “And the servant abideth not in the house for ever: but the Son abideth ever.”

John 8:36 — “If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.”

B. Who, to whom, why

Who speaks? Jesus. To whom? Those Jews which believed on him. Why? Because belief that will not continue in His word is not yet “disciples indeed,” and because they answered from Abraham and from a claim never to have been in bondage, while He was speaking of the servant of sin.

Continue is the condition. If ye continue in my word — then disciples indeed — and ye shall know the truth — and the truth shall make you free. Knowledge here is not a slogan about truth. It is the knowing that comes to those who remain in His word. That knowing is the knowledge section VII defined, applied to His word: perceive it, learn it, reason it, remain in it.

They protest from pedigree. Abraham's seed. Never in bondage. He does not argue politics with them. He names sin as bondage. Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin. The servant does not abide in the house for ever. The Son does. Freedom, then, is the Son’s freedom: if the Son shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.

C. Scripture set with Hebrews 5:11-14

Hold John 8:31-36 with Hebrews 5:11-14. Dull hearing will not get you that freedom. Unskill in the word of righteousness will not get you that freedom. A man who will not continue in the word cannot claim the freedom the word promises. A babe who will not be exercised cannot discern the bondage he is still in.

The opening of this book is therefore not a motto. Truth makes free where the word is continued in. The cover line is not a substitute for John 8. The platform line is not a substitute for John 8.

D. Distinction, principle, charge

Distinction: freedom from remaining in His word, over against being the servant of sin, versus a political cry versus a mood versus a pedigree that says “we were never in bondage.”

Principle: you shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free, if you continue in His word and if the Son makes you free. That freedom is from the bondage of sin.

Reasoning: if they could have been free by Abraham, He would not have said “if ye continue.” If they could have been free by denying bondage, He would not have said “servant of sin.” If a motto could free you, this school could print the cover and close the book.

Application: free from what, in John 8, if you continue in His word? Answer from the Scripture set. Servant of sin. Then the Son. Then free indeed. Do not write “free from negativity.” Do not write “free from religion.” Write what He wrote against.

Charge: write John 8:31-36. Then name one word of His you will continue in this week — a verse, written in full — and write what continuing will look like at three hours, and what it will look like if you are intensive. Same verse. Different labour. Same freedom offered. No second truth.

IX. THE SIX FIRST PRINCIPLES

A. The verses

Hebrews 6:1 — “Therefore leaving the principles of the doctrine of Christ, let us go on unto perfection; not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works, and of faith toward God,”

Hebrews 6:2 — “Of the doctrine of baptisms, and of laying on of hands, and of resurrection of the dead, and of eternal judgment.”

These six are the Year-1 courses of Foundation School. They are not slogans. They are not a seventh course in disguise. They are not to be merged.

1. Repentance from dead works.
2. Faith toward God.
3. The doctrine of baptisms.
4. Laying on of hands.
5. Resurrection of the dead.
6. Eternal judgment.

B. Leaving, not skipping, not relaying

Therefore leaving — the therefore is the argument of chapter 5. Because you ought to be teachers, because milk-users are babes, because strong meat belongs to the exercised, leave the principles as a foundation already to be built on, and go on unto perfection.

Not laying again the foundation. The six are a foundation. A foundation is laid once and then bears the house. You do not pour it every spring and call the pouring a life with God. You also do not refuse to pour it and then decorate the air.

A man who has never laid them is not “leaving” them. He is skipping them. This chapter is the gate. Chapter 2 opens the first of the six. The remaining chapters open the rest, in the order Hebrews names them. You will not be offered a rearranged year to suit a preference. The writer named the order.

C. What each stone is, at the gate

You do not need Chapters 2 through 7 before you can name the six. You need this much, so you do not merge them.

Repentance from dead works is a change of mind over sin and its cause, not a regret of consequences only. Chapter 2 will open it.

Faith toward God is credence that defines the state of sons. Chapter 3 will open it.

The doctrine of baptisms is plural. Three are essential for believers. Only one of those three saves the soul. Chapter 4 will open it. Water will not be this first stone.

Laying on of hands has nine occasions. It is resultant, not a substitute for the first three. Chapter 5 will open it.

Resurrection of the dead is spiritual and material, and the material is of the body. Chapter 6 will open it.

Eternal judgment is eternal, with a book, with deaths that must stay three, with prisons that are not one room called Hell. Chapter 7 will open it.

Do not teach Chapter 7 in Chapter 1. Do not teach Chapter 2 as if it were all six. Name them. Keep them. Go on when they are laid.

D. The year

Fifty-two weeks. The Walk about three hours a week. Intensive about eight. Same six. Course 1, nine weeks. Course 2, nine. Course 3, eight. Course 4, eight. Course 5, nine. Course 6, nine.

A certificate, when issued, is for completing a program, not for buying a book, not for clicking a lesson. Written charges, an examination per course, a week-52 final: that is the labour the school will ask. Mid-year and capstone demonstrations, if they come later, will not replace this foundation.

Enrolment in the school program grants the six courses and this textbook. It does not grant the companion library. Companions named in later chapters are books, not Year-1 courses. The Power of Salvation will be named in Chapter 2 as directed reading, not as a seventh course.

E. Charge

Write the six in order from memory. Write one sentence for each that does not steal a sentence from a later chapter you have not yet reasoned. Then write what you will not do: you will not add a seventh, you will not merge two, you will not call skipping “leaving,” you will not call relaying “growth.”

X. IF GOD PERMIT

A. The hinge

Hebrews 6:3 — “And this will we do, if God permit.”

The banner of runs from Hebrews 5:11 to 6:3. Verse 3 is the hinge after the six are named. We will go on to perfection — if God permit.

This is not a seventh principle. It is not a seventh course. It is the writer’s dependence after he has named the work. The six are in 6:1-2. Verse 3 is the sentence that binds the going-on to God.

B. Dependence, not fatalism

That is not fatalism. It is dependence. The writer does not treat maturity as a human schedule you can force. He treats it as a work we intend, under permission.

“This will we do” is intention. The writer is not shrinking from the six or from perfection. “If God permit” is the limit of the intention. You may enrol in a fifty-two week program. You cannot enrol God.

Permission here is not an excuse for sloth. Spoudazō remains a command. Dull hearing remains an indictment. Apeiros remains a diagnosis. The man who will not labour has not been refused permission. He has refused labour. The man who labours still cannot treat the year as a machine that outputs perfection at week 52.

C. Unfinished foundations

Do not call unfinished foundations “perfection.” Do not call a certificate “if God permit” as if paper were the hinge. Do not call an intensive hour-count permission. Hours are labour. Permission is God’s.

Walk the year as labour. Ask for permission to go on. Lay the six. Then go on — if God permit.

The next chapter takes up repentance from dead works. Do not read it as a feeling. Read it as the first stone.

D. Charge

Write Hebrews 6:1-3 as one Scripture set. Mark the six names. Mark “if God permit.” Write what you intend this year, and what you cannot force. Then put the first stone in front of you and stop calling the gate the house.

XI. WORD DRILL LABOUR

This section does not add doctrine. It assigns the labour by which section VII becomes more than a definition.

A. The verse you will write

Write Hebrews 5:12 in full, by hand, from the KJV, until you can do it without looking. Then write 2 Timothy 2:15 the same way. Then write John 8:31-32 the same way.

If you are on The Walk, that is the week’s writing of verses, with the reasoning below in tight paragraphs. If you are on The Intensive, write also Hebrews 5:11-14 and 6:1-3 as one stretch, and expand every reasoning sentence into a paragraph a babe could follow.

B. Reason the words

On 2 Timothy 2:15, reason approved. Unto whom? God. For what? A workman who needeth not to be ashamed. Approved is not a mood and not a crowd.

Reason workman. The work is the word of truth. A workman can be ashamed. Hardness sits in the same chapter. The word of God is not bound.

Reason rightly dividing. The word can be divided wrongly. Right division keeps the Scripture set and the distinction. Wrong division merges the six, or skips them, or trades the graphē for a likeness.

On Hebrews 5:12, reason ought, again, become, milk, strong meat, first principles, oracles of God. Each word does work. If you cannot say the work, you have recited.

On John 8:31-36, reason continue, disciples indeed, know, truth, free, servant of sin, the Son, free indeed. Hold them as one argument. Do not take 8:32 to a banner and leave 8:34 on the table.

C. The method, once more

Scripture in full. Term as defined here. Context: who, to whom, why. Scripture set held together. Distinction. Principle. Reasoning. Application. Charge.

That is how you will read every chapter. That is how you will write. A student at three hours a week can do this on one Scripture set and be honest. A student at eight hours can do this on the whole chapter and be honest. Neither may replace the method with a summary.

XII. WHAT THIS CHAPTER WILL NOT DO

It will not treat this textbook as a second Bible.

It will not confuse the cover line of the book with the house line of the platform.

It will not trade the graphē for substitute religious likenesses.

It will not skip the foundation and call the skip maturity.

It will not relay the foundation every year and call the relaying growth.

It will not treat milk after time as humility.

It will not treat ἄπειρος (apeiros) as lack of a platform.

It will not treat νήπιος (nēpios) as a term of endearment.

It will not treat knowledge as quotation.

It will not treat John 8:32 as a motto.

It will not add a seventh Year-1 course.

It will not treat Hebrews 6:3 as a seventh principle.

It will not give you a second doctrine for the intensive clock.

XIII. LABOUR FOR THE WALK AND THE INTENSIVE

Same doctrine. Same six. Same chapter. Different hours.

The Walk — about three hours a week. Read this chapter in two sittings. Write the charges in sections I, III, V, VI, and VIII as five tight paragraphs. Write Hebrews 5:12 and 2 Timothy 2:15 by hand. Name the six. Name the two marks of babes. That is enough writing for the gate if the writing is honest.

Intensive — about eight hours a week. Read this chapter until you can teach it. Write the charges in every section. Write Hebrews 5:11-14 and 6:1-3 by hand. Write John 8:31-36 by hand. Write one page on graphē versus religious substitute. Write one page on ἄπειρος (apeiros) and νήπιος (nēpios) without using the word “basically.” Write the 2 Timothy 2:15 drill in six sentences that reason, not six sentences that repeat. Sit with a babe and teach 5:12 until he can say “ought,” “again,” and “become.”

Both: you are not finished because you reached section XIII. You are finished when you can teach the gate without a slogan, and when you can ask permission to go on without calling an unlaid foundation perfection.

The first stone is the next chapter. Do not open it as a feeling. Open it as a man who has heard that the scripture cannot be broken, and that you ought, by this time, to be a teacher of the beginning.

chapters.title: Repentance from Dead Works
chapters.body:
Hebrews 6:1 — “Therefore leaving the principles of the doctrine of Christ, let us go on unto perfection; not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works, and of faith toward God,”

This is the first stone. If this stone is a slogan, the year is a slogan.

Chapter 1 opened the gate. This chapter lays the first of the six. You will not be given a feeling in the place of the Scripture set, an eighth repent-word, Matthew 16 as the narrative of Hell, or a second saviour.

A student at three hours a week must have something to sit with. An intensive student uses the same text with longer writing. The doctrine does not change with the clock.

I. ΜΕΤΆΝΟΙΑ FROM ΝΕΚΡῶΝ ἜΡΓΩΝ

A. The heading
